NoteOverview



This week we focus on two strands of learning:

The linear model with interactions

In Weeks 7 and 8 you learned how to use the linear model to predict one variable from one or more other variables, including a categorical variable.
This week you will learn how to test whether the effect of one predictor is different for different values of another predictor. This is called an interaction.
Psychologists often expect effects to vary between groups of people, or for people with different scores on a third variable. Interactions let us examine this.
We will do all this in the context of the Clearly Understood project on how easy or difficult people find it to understand written health information.

title: 9. Week 9 - The linear model (with interaction)
text:
Lectures






Note



Please note that Rob may mention a different module code or different week during the lectures. I’ve reviewed the material and the content is entirely relevant to the current module.








Tip



In week 9, we aim to further develop skills in analysing and in visualising psychological data. We will do so in the context of the Clearly Understood project.
We will face what the lectures call the real challenge in psychological science:

People vary
Effects vary
Results vary

Because the effects that interest us can be expected to vary, we need to be able to investigate how they vary. We do this using linear models that include interaction effects.

If we think that the shape or size of an effect is different in different groups of people, or for different values of a third variable (a moderator),
then we are thinking about an interaction effect.

When we report a model that includes an interaction, we still report the model we specified, the model fit statistics (F, R-squared) and the coefficient estimates. We now also need to describe how the effect of one predictor changes, given different values of another predictor. Plots of model predictions help us to do this.








Tip



Before you go on to the activities in Section 4, watch the lectures:


The lecture for part A for this week is presented in four short parts. You can view video recordings of the lectures using Panopto, by clicking on the links shown following.

Introduction (9 minutes): The real challenge in psychological science (people vary, effects vary, results vary); variation, uncertainty, and working with the limits of samples.



The Clearly Understood project – questions and analyses (11 minutes): Critical thinking – what effects can vary, how effects can vary, and theoretical reasons why effects might vary.



Coding models with interactions (19 minutes): Revision on linear models; coding models that do or do not include interactions; identifying the key information in the results; and making sense of what we see.



Interactions between numeric variables and factors (13 minutes): Numeric variables and factors as predictors; coding, plotting, interpreting and reporting interactions between numeric variables and factors. Summary of key lessons.








Tip



The slides presented in the videos can be downloaded as a web page. You can download the web page .html file and click on it to open it in any browser (e.g., Chrome, Edge or Safari). The slide images are high quality so the file is quite big (13 MB) and may take a few seconds to download.



The slides


The lectures have four main areas of focus
1. The real challenge in psychological science
We connect (1.) the fact that psychological and social processes vary to (2.) the uncertainties we face when we try to draw conclusions from limited samples.






Tip



What makes psychological science challenging:

People vary
Effects vary
Results vary



2. Critical thinking
So far, we have looked at the impact on understanding of differences between individuals in attributes like vocabulary knowledge. Now, we consider the possibility that the effect of one predictor could itself vary.






Tip



We can develop our critical thinking skills by considering:

What effects can vary
How effects can vary

We discuss the kinds of theoretical assumptions that may lead psychologists to hypothesise interaction effects.


3. Coding models with interactions
We build on what we know about coding linear models with multiple predictors to code models that include interaction effects.






Tip



We build skills by looking at:

the code we use;
the key information in the results, where to find it, and how to interpret it;
the different ways in which we can present and interpret interactions.



4. Interactions between numeric variables and factors
The effect of a numeric variable (like reading strategy) can differ depending on another numeric variable (like health literacy). An effect can also differ between groups, which we code using categorical variables (factors) like education level. We look at how to code, interpret and report interactions between numeric variables and factors.

Pre-lab activities
After having watched the lectures you’ll be in a good position to try these activities. Completing them before you attend your lab session will help you to consolidate your learning and help move through the lab activities more smoothly.

Pre-lab activity 1: Predict before you look
In the lectures, Rob describes two theories about how the effect of health literacy on understanding might depend on vocabulary knowledge. In the lab, we ask a similar question about reading strategy:

Is the effect of reading strategy (FACTOR3) on accuracy of understanding (mean.acc) different for people with different levels of health literacy (HLVA)?

Here are two possible theories:

Theory 1: the effect of reading strategy is larger (the slope is steeper) for people with higher health literacy, because people who know more about health can make more use of a good reading strategy.
Theory 2: the effect of reading strategy is smaller (the slope is shallower) for people with higher health literacy, because people who already understand health information well have less room to improve.

Before the lab, write down your predictions:

Which theory do you think is more likely? Why?
Do you expect the effect of reading strategy to be different for people with further education and people with higher education? If so, in which direction?

Keep your predictions: you will compare them with the results in Steps 5 and 6 of the lab.






Tip



In the lab, we include education level (EDUCATION) as a categorical predictor, as we did in Week 8. If you need to, look back at Step 9 of the Week 8 lab to remind yourself what a reference level is.




Pre-lab activity 2: See how slope estimates vary between samples
Have a look at this app on sampling variation in linear models by Rob Davies.
The app simulates data for a linear model with one predictor. It shows the slope estimate for one sample, alongside four more samples drawn from the same population, and two piles of 100 simulated studies: one where there is no effect in the population, and one where there is an effect.






Important



The app runs in Chrome or Edge, not in Safari. The first time you open it, it downloads the software it needs (60-90 MB), which can take up to a minute.


Try the following:

Compare the slope estimates in the different samples from the same population. Click Draw new samples a few times.
Change N per study to make the samples smaller, then larger, and draw new samples each time.
Look at the pile of studies where there is no effect in the population.

Pre-lab activity questions:

How much do the slope estimates vary between samples drawn from the same population?
What happens to this variation when the samples are smaller or larger?
In the pile of studies where there is no effect in the population, do all the slope estimates equal zero?

Keep your answers in mind for Steps 2 and 8 of the lab. When we look for an interaction, we compare slopes estimated in parts of a sample, so this variation matters.

We’ll work with an example script called 4141_wk9_lab.qmd. This is a Quarto document.

You can download the files here: 4141_wk9_lab.zip. Usually they will be saved in your ‘Downloads’ folder.

text:
Lab activities

Lab activity 1: What makes it easy or difficult for people to understand written health information?
We will do our practical lab work to develop your skills in the context of the Clearly Understood project.






Important



The research questions we are focussing on today are:

What person attributes predict success in understanding health information?
How can the effects of person attributes vary, in different groups of people, or for different values of a third variable (a moderator)?



This week, we work with a larger dataset. It combines the data from the two studies of adults in the UK, including the study two data you used in Weeks 7 and 8, with data collected from Lancaster first-year psychology students in a previous year. Studying interactions usually needs more data than studying the effect of one predictor.
We focus on one effect: the effect of reading strategy (FACTOR3) on accuracy of understanding (mean.acc). We ask whether this effect is different:

for people with different levels of health literacy (HLVA), a numeric variable;
for people with different levels of education (EDUCATION), a categorical variable.







TipWhere are the download links?



Links to the files to be downloaded are in the Pre-lab activities section under Getting ready.



Aims of the activity
We are going to:

Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio – using rm() and library()
Read in and inspect the data – using read_csv(), summary() and as.factor()
Visualise possible interactions – using geom_smooth(), facet_wrap() and cut_number()
Centre numeric predictors and fit a model without an interaction
Fit and plot an interaction between two numeric predictors – using lm() with *, and ggpredict()
Fit and plot an interaction between a numeric predictor and a categorical predictor
Report the results of a linear model with an interaction
Extension: How robust is the interaction?







Tip



Steps 1 to 7 are the main lab activity. Step 8 is an extension: do it if you have time, or after the lab.








ImportantHow to use the Quarto document?



All instructions and guidance (including hints and code snippets) for lab activities are presented on this handbook page.
The Quarto document is largely empty, only containing a copy of the section headers and the actions to remind you of what you are meant to do. Sometimes there are questions associated with the code you’ve written or the output that follows from it. These can also be found on both the handbook page and in the Quarto document.
How to complete the lab activity and use the Quarto script:

Open the handbook pages in a separate window or tab and navigate to Lab activities.
Read the instructions on the handbook page for each step.
Carry out the actions, by inserting a code chunk in the Quarto document, below each action.
If there are any questions associated with that step, please try to answer them. You can write your answer in the Quarto document, as plain text. Answers to the questions will be shared after the last lab session has taken place (on Thursday afternoon).
After having carried out an action, written a code chunk and answered any questions, go back to the handbook page and read the next bit of instruction, until you get to the next action.
If you are stuck: Have a look at the ‘Hints’ and ‘Code’ snippets on the handbook page.
If you are still stuck: Ask for help (your peers on your table, the GTA or lecturer in the lab session, via the Moodle Q&A forum, during Friday’s live online Q&A).

If you’d like to watch a demonstration of this, have a look at the video at the start of Lab activity 3 of Week 5 (here).




Step 1: Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio

Action: In a new code chunk, add the code to empty the R environment. Then add the code to load the relevant libraries. We need the following ones: here, tidyverse, easystats and ggeffects.







TipCode





rm(list=ls())

library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(easystats)
library(ggeffects)





Step 2: Read in and inspect the data
The data file for this lab activity is all.data.csv. It has the same columns as the data file we used in Weeks 7 and 8:

participant_ID participant code;
mean.acc average accuracy of response to questions testing understanding of health guidance (varies between 0-1);
mean.self average self-rated accuracy of understanding of health guidance (varies between 1-9);
study variable coding for what study the data were collected in (study.one, study.two or PSYC122, the student data);
AGE age in years;
SHIPLEY vocabulary knowledge test score (varies between 0-40);
HLVA health literacy test score (varies between 1-16);
FACTOR3 reading strategy survey score (varies between 0-80);
GENDER gender code (here, Female or Male);
EDUCATION education level code (here, Further or Higher);
ETHNICITY ethnicity (Office National Statistics categories) code.


Action 1. In a new code chunk use read_csv() and here() to read in the data file. Give the data object a distinct name, e.g. all.data. Then use summary() to get an overview of the data.







TipCode





all.data <- read_csv(here("4141_wk9_lab", "all.data.csv"))

summary(all.data)



In the summary, EDUCATION is shown as Class: character, so we cannot see how many participants are in each group. If we change it into a factor, summary() will count the participants at each level.

Action 2. Change EDUCATION into a factor using as.factor(). Then use summary() again.







TipCode





all.data$EDUCATION <- as.factor(all.data$EDUCATION)

summary(all.data)

all.data$EDUCATION picks out the EDUCATION column of all.data.
as.factor() changes the variable into a factor, and the assignment arrow <- puts the result back in the same column.




Questions Step 2

How many participants are in the dataset, and how many are in each level of EDUCATION?
In Weeks 7 and 8 we used data from 172 participants. Why do you think we need a larger dataset to study interactions?







NoteHint





Think about what you saw in the app in Pre-lab activity 2: how did the slope estimates change when the samples were smaller?





Step 3: Visualise possible interactions
An interaction means that the effect of one predictor (here, the slope of the association between FACTOR3 and mean.acc) is different for different values of another variable. We can look for this by drawing the same scatterplot separately for different groups of participants.

Action 1. Draw a scatterplot of the association between FACTOR3 (x-axis) and mean.acc (y-axis), with a separate panel for each level of EDUCATION.







TipCode





ggplot(data = all.data, aes(x = FACTOR3, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Reading strategy (FACTOR3)", y = "Mean accuracy") +
  xlim(0, 80) + ylim(0, 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ EDUCATION)

geom_smooth(method = "lm") adds a linear model line (the trend) with its 95% confidence interval as a grey band. R will show the message `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x': this is not an error.
facet_wrap(~ EDUCATION) splits the data by EDUCATION and draws a separate panel for each level. See the facet_wrap() reference page.




To do the same for a numeric variable like HLVA, we first need to split the participants into groups based on their HLVA scores.

Action 2. Use cut_number() to split the participants into three groups of roughly equal size (low, mid and high HLVA scores). Then draw the scatterplot with a separate panel for each group.







TipCode





all.data$HLVA_splits <- cut_number(all.data$HLVA, 3)

ggplot(data = all.data, aes(x = FACTOR3, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Reading strategy (FACTOR3)", y = "Mean accuracy") +
  xlim(0, 80) + ylim(0, 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ HLVA_splits, nrow = 1, labeller = label_both)

cut_number(all.data$HLVA, 3) orders the participants by their HLVA score and splits them into three groups. The result is stored in a new column, HLVA_splits. See the cut_number() reference page.
nrow = 1 puts the panels side by side, and labeller = label_both shows the variable name as well as the group in each panel label.
Where the splits fall depends on the scores in the sample.




Questions Step 3

Compare the trend lines for Further and Higher education. Does the effect of reading strategy look different?
Compare the trend lines for the three HLVA groups. What do the labels at the top of the panels (e.g. [2,8]) tell you, and how does the slope change from low to high HLVA?



Step 4: Centre numeric predictors and fit a model without an interaction
Before we fit models with interactions, we centre the numeric predictors. Centring a variable means subtracting the variable’s mean from every score, so that a centred score of 0 is the average score.
Why do this? In a model with an interaction, the estimate for each predictor on its own is its effect when the other predictor is 0. For our variables, 0 is not a useful value: nobody in the sample scored 0 on FACTOR3 (the lowest score is 9) or on HLVA (the lowest is 2). After centring, each estimate shows the effect for a person with an average score on the other predictor. Centring does not change the interaction estimate, its significance, or how well the model fits.

Action 1. In a new code chunk, create centred versions of FACTOR3 and HLVA.







TipCode





all.data$FACTOR3_centered <- all.data$FACTOR3 - mean(all.data$FACTOR3, na.rm = TRUE)
all.data$HLVA_centered <- all.data$HLVA - mean(all.data$HLVA, na.rm = TRUE)

mean(all.data$FACTOR3, na.rm = TRUE) calculates the mean of FACTOR3. na.rm = TRUE tells R to ignore missing values, if there are any.
Subtracting the mean from the column gives the centred score for every participant, which we store in a new column.





Action 2. Fit a model with mean.acc as the outcome and the centred FACTOR3 and HLVA as predictors, without an interaction. Then get the model summary.







TipCode





model.1 <- lm(mean.acc ~ FACTOR3_centered + HLVA_centered, data = all.data)
summary(model.1)



Questions Step 4

What does a FACTOR3_centered score of 0 mean? What does a score of -10 mean?
What does the intercept estimate mean in this model?







NoteHint






The intercept is the predicted outcome when all the predictors are 0.
Optional: fit the same model with the uncentred FACTOR3 and HLVA and compare the two summaries. What changes and what stays the same?






Step 5: Fit and plot an interaction between two numeric predictors
To include an interaction in a model, we separate the predictors with * instead of +:
lm(outcome ~ predictor.X*predictor.Z, data = data.set)
This gives a model with the effect of each predictor and the interaction between them. In the model summary, the interaction is shown as predictor.X:predictor.Z.

Action 1. In a new code chunk, fit a model with mean.acc as the outcome and the interaction between the centred FACTOR3 and HLVA. Then get the model summary.







TipCode





model.2 <- lm(mean.acc ~ FACTOR3_centered * HLVA_centered, data = all.data)
summary(model.2)









NoteWhat do the estimates mean?




FACTOR3_centered: the effect (slope) of reading strategy for a person with an average HLVA score (HLVA_centered = 0).
HLVA_centered: the effect of health literacy for a person with an average FACTOR3 score.
FACTOR3_centered:HLVA_centered: the interaction. It shows how much the slope of FACTOR3 changes for each one-point increase in HLVA. A positive estimate means the reading strategy slope gets steeper as HLVA increases; a negative estimate means it gets shallower.



Interactions are easier to understand if we plot them. We use ggpredict(), as in Week 8, but now name two predictors in terms.

Action 2. Use ggpredict() and plot() to plot the predictions of the model for FACTOR3_centered, at different values of HLVA_centered.







TipCode





dat.int.1 <- ggpredict(model.2, terms = c("FACTOR3_centered", "HLVA_centered"))
plot(dat.int.1) +
  theme_bw() +
  ylim(0, 1)

The first predictor named in terms goes on the x-axis. The second is the moderator: ggpredict() draws a separate line for three of its values, the mean (0) and one standard deviation below and above the mean (-2.19 and 2.19).
In the lecture slides, these plots are made with plot_model() from the sjPlot library. plot_model() uses ggpredict() to calculate the predictions, so the plots show the same thing.
The message Scale for y is already present is not an error: ylim() has replaced the y-axis that plot() set.




Questions Step 5

Which estimate tells you about the interaction? Is the interaction significant?
What does the sign of the interaction estimate tell you? Check your answer against the plot.
Do the results support Theory 1 or Theory 2 from Pre-lab activity 1?



Step 6: Fit and plot an interaction between a numeric predictor and a categorical predictor
Interactions with a categorical predictor are coded in the same way.

Action 1. Fit a model with mean.acc as the outcome and the interaction between FACTOR3_centered and EDUCATION. Then get the model summary.







TipCode





model.3 <- lm(mean.acc ~ FACTOR3_centered*EDUCATION, data = all.data)
summary(model.3)









NoteWhat do the estimates mean?



Further is the reference level (it comes first in the alphabet), so:

FACTOR3_centered: the slope of reading strategy for participants with Further education.
EDUCATIONHigher: the difference in predicted accuracy between Higher and Further education, for a person with an average FACTOR3 score.
FACTOR3_centered:EDUCATIONHigher: the interaction. It shows how much steeper (if positive) or shallower (if negative) the reading strategy slope is for Higher compared with Further education.




Action 2. Use ggpredict() and plot() to plot the predictions of the model for FACTOR3_centered, for each level of EDUCATION.







TipCode





dat.int.2 <- ggpredict(model.3, terms = c("FACTOR3_centered", "EDUCATION"))
plot(dat.int.2) +
  theme_bw() +
  ylim(0, 1)



Questions Step 6

Is the interaction significant?
What is the slope of reading strategy for participants with Further education, and for participants with Higher education? Describe the interaction in words.
What does the EDUCATIONHigher estimate mean, and is it significant?
Stretch question: the lecture shows the same model fitted with the uncentred reading strategy scores. There, the EDUCATIONHigher estimate is -0.199 and significant (p = .017). Why is it so different from your estimate?







NoteHint






For question b: the slope for Higher education is the slope for Further education plus the interaction estimate.
For question d: what value of reading strategy does the EDUCATIONHigher estimate refer to in each model?






Step 7: Report the results of a linear model with an interaction

Action: In your Quarto document, write a short report of the model you fitted in Step 6. Write it as plain text, not in a code chunk. Use the example in the lectures and the template in the Hint.







NoteHint





Fill in the gaps ... using the model summary from Step 6.

We fitted a linear model with mean comprehension accuracy as the outcome and reading strategy (FACTOR3, centred on its mean), education level and their interaction as predictors. The model is significant overall, F(…, …) = …, p …, and explains …% of variance (adjusted R² = …). For participants with further education, accuracy increased with higher reading strategy scores (b = …, t = …, p …). At the average reading strategy score, accuracy did … differ between participants with higher and further education (b = …, t = …, p …). A … interaction (b = …, t = …, p …) indicates that the reading strategy effect was … for participants with higher education.


As in Week 8, report the estimates as b.
In a model with an interaction, describe each estimate for what it is: for example, the FACTOR3_centered estimate is the reading strategy slope for the reference level (Further), not for everyone.






Step 8: Extension – How robust is the interaction?
Look again at the Further panel of the first plot in Step 3. One participant has a reading strategy score of 9, far below everyone else (the next lowest score is 29), and high accuracy (0.95). In Week 5, you looked at how unusual data points can affect a correlation. The same can happen in a linear model.

Action: Fit the model from Step 6 again, without this participant. Then get the model summary.







TipCode





all.data.check <- filter(all.data, FACTOR3 > 9)

model.4 <- lm(mean.acc ~ FACTOR3_centered * EDUCATION, data = all.data.check)
summary(model.4)

filter(all.data, FACTOR3 > 9) keeps only the rows (participants) for whom FACTOR3 is greater than 9, and we store the result as a new dataset, all.data.check. The original all.data is not changed.




Questions Step 8

Is the interaction still significant without this participant? How has the interaction estimate changed?
What does this tell you about how much confidence to place in the interaction? Should we remove this participant from the analysis?

Lectures






Note



Please note that Rob may mention a different module code or different week during the lectures. I’ve reviewed the material and the content is entirely relevant to the current module.








Tip



In week 7, we aim to further develop skills in analysing and in visualising psychological data. We will do so in the context of the Clearly Understood project.
We will aim to answer the research question: What person attributes in adult readers predict success in understanding written health information?
Research questions like this can be examined using linear models.
When we do these analyses, we will need to think about how we report the results and decide:

is the association significant?
does the association reflect a positive or negative relationship between outcome and predictor?
is the association relatively strong or weak?

Our thinking, and our decision-making, will be helped by developing our data visualisation skills. At every stage, as we work, we will visualize the data to understand the shape of the relationships we may observe or predict.


The lecture for part A for this week is presented in four short parts. You can view video recordings of the lectures using Panopto, by clicking on the links shown following.

Overview (19 minutes): What we are doing in Week 7 – thinking critically about predicting people.



Using linear models to do prediction (11 minutes): How we answer live research questions by using linear models to predict behaviour.



How linear models work (9 minutes): How we can visualize and think about predictions, and about the difference between what we predict and what we observe when we study people.



Interpreting, reporting and visualizing linear model results (15 minutes): Identifying, interpreting and communicating the key statistics.








Tip



The slides presented in the videos can be downloaded either as a web page. You can download the web page .html file and click on it to open it in any browser (e.g., Chrome, Edge or Safari). The slide images are high quality so the file is quite big and may take a few seconds to download.



The slides

B. The mini research project
If you haven’t already, make sure you watch the overview video on the mini research project and the video on what makes a good research question on the project page.
After that, make sure to watch the videos introducing the Gorilla platform and on how to build a questionnaire on Gorilla.

Overview (~9 minutes) Key information on what you’ll be expected to do, a rough timeline and how it links to assessment. You can view this video on the project page here.
What makes a good research question (~16 minutes) The video discusses why articulating a good research question is important and how to check that you’ve got one? It also discusses how to write hypotheses to go with your research question. We went over this during the week 6 lab session. You can view this video on the project page here.

Pre-lab activities



After having watched the lectures and read the textbook chapter you’ll be in a good position to try these activities. Completing them before you attend your lab session will help you to consolidate your learning and help move through the lab activities more smoothly.

Pre-lab activity 1: Visualising the regression line
Have a look at this visualisation of the regression line by Ryan Safner.
In this shiny app, you see a randomly-generated set of data points (within specific parameters, to keep the graph scaled properly). You can choose a slope and intercept for the regression line by using the sliders. The graph also displays the residuals as dashed red lines. Moving the slope or the intercept too much causes the generated line to create much larger residuals. The shiny app also calculates the sum of squared errors (SSE) and the standard error of the regression (SER), which calculates the average size of the error (the red numbers). These numbers reflect how well the regression line fits the data, but you don’t need to worry about those for now.
In the app he uses the equation Y = aX + b in which b is the intercept and a is the slope.
Pre-lab activity questions:

Change the slider for the intercept. How does it change the regression line?
Change the slider for the slope. How does it change the regression line?
What happens to the residuals (the red dashed lines) when you change the slope and the intercept of the regression line?



Pre-lab activity 2: Measuring mind wandering and screen time
With your group you need to decide how to measure the variables you’ve specified in your research question. In this module we focus on using questionnaires to measure constructs.
To prepare for discussion within your group, please read (some of) the papers listed on the project page, in the section on Measuring mind wandering and screen time here. These are examples of questionnaires you could use. There is also a book chapter that provides more background on questionnaire research.


Pre-lab activity 3: Getting setup on Gorilla
You will build the study on the Gorilla platform. Each student will need to create an account. This is free to do. To create an account, click on this link and follow the instruction.






ImportantUse your Lancaster University email address



Please make sure to use your university email address (ending in ‘@lancaster.ac.uk’) to create your Gorilla account.




Pre-lab activity 4: Getting ready


To complete this week’s lab activity you will need several files:

We’ll work with an example script called 4141_wk7_lab.qmd. This is a Quarto document.
We’ll also need a data file names study-two-general-participants.csv.

You can download the files here: 4141_wk7_lab.zip. Usually they will be saved in your ‘Downloads’ folder.
Next, upload the zip-folder as it is to your Files space on the R-server (bottom right quadrant; no need to extract the files first).
Finally, open the example script by clicking on the file called 4141_wk7_lab.qmd in the Files space on the R-server.
You are now ready to start work on the lab activities.

text:
Lab activities




Lab activity 1: What makes it easy or difficult for people to understand written health information?
We will do our practical lab work to develop your skills in the context of the Clearly Understood project.






Important



The research question we are focussing on today is:

What person attributes predict success in understanding health information?









TipWhere are the download links?



Links to the files to be downloaded are in the Pre-lab activities section under Getting ready.



Aims of the activity
We are going to:

Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio – using library()
Read in the data file – using read_csv()
Inspect the data – using head() and summary()
Draw histograms to examine the distributions of variables – using ggplot() and geom_histogram()
Practice editing the appearance of a histogram plot step-by-step
Create scatterplots to examine the association between some variables – using ggplot() and geom_point()
Edit the appearance of each plot step-by-step
Examine the correlations between the outcome variable and predictor variables
Examine the relation between outcome mean accuracy (mean.acc) and each of the potential predictors: SHIPLEY, HLVA and AGE
Use a model we have fitted to plot model predictions







ImportantHow to use the Quarto document?



All instructions and guidance (including hints and code snippets) for lab activities are presented on this handbook page.
The Quarto document is largely empty, only containing a copy of the section headers and the actions to remind you of what you are meant to do. Sometimes there are questions associated with the code you’ve written or the output that follows from it. These can also be found on both the handbook page and in the Quarto document.
How to complete the lab activity and use the Quarto script:

Open the handbook pages in a separate window or tab and navigate to Lab activities.
Read the instructions on the handbook page for each step.
Carry out the actions, by inserting a code chunk in the Quarto document, below each action.
If there are any questions associated with that step, please try to answer them. You can write your answer in the Quarto document, as plain text. Answers to the questions will be shared after the last lab session has taken place (on Thursday afternoon).
After having carried out an action, written a code chunk and answered any questions, go back to the handbook page and read the next bit of instruction, until you get to the next action.
If you are stuck: Have a look at the ‘Hints’ and ‘Code’ snippets on the handbook page.
If you are still stuck: Ask for help (your peers on your table, the GTA or lecturer in the lab session, via the Moodle Q&A forum, during Friday’s live online Q&A).

If you’d like to watch a demonstration of this, have a look at the video at the start of Lab activity 3 of Week 5 (here).




Step 1: Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio
Before we can do anything, we need tell R what packages we want to use.

Action: In a new code chunk, add the code to load the relevant libraries. We need the following ones: here, tidyverse and easystats. If you are unsure, you can look at the ‘Hint’ below for a clue by expanding it.







NoteHint





Use the library()function. Remember to put it inside a ‘code chunk’ in your script. The name of the package goes inside the brackets. Repeat for each package.





Step 2: Read in the data file
Now we need to read in the data. The data file we need for this lab activity is called: study-two-general-participants.csv.

Action: In a new code chunk use read_csv() to read in the data file named study-two-general-participants.csv. Remeber to tell R where to find the file and what it is called. Make sure you’ve run the code chunk. Then, check that you can see the ‘object’ in the Environment (top right quadrant) for the file you read in.


When you code this, you can choose your own file name, but be sure to give the data object you create a distinct name e.g. study.two.gen.







NoteHint





dataframe <- read_csv(here("filepath to folder", "filename.extension))
Your code should include:

dataframe: the name of the object you want to save the data in (such as study.two.gen)
<- : assignment arrow
read_csv() : the read_csv() function
here(): the here() function
“filepath to folder”: the folders that you need to point R to starting from whereever here starts
“filename.extension”: the name of the datafile, including the extension










TipCode





study.two.gen<- read_csv(here("4141_wk7_lab", "study-two-general-participants.csv"))





Step 3: Inspect the data
It is always a good idea to have a look at the data. You can do this by clicking on the object in the Environment quadrant. This will open the file in the Source quadrant.
You can see the columns:

participant_ID participant code;
mean.acc average accuracy of response to questions testing understanding of health guidance (varies between 0-1);
mean.self average self-rated accuracy of understanding of health guidance (varies between 1-9);
study variable coding for what study the data were collected in
AGE age in years;
HLVA health literacy test score (varies between 1-16);
SHIPLEY vocabulary knowledge test score (varies between 0-40);
FACTOR3 reading strategy survey score (varies between 0-80);
GENDER gender code;
EDUCATION education level code;
ETHNICITY ethnicity (Office National Statistics categories) code.

You can also use code to get an overview:

The head() function will show you the first few rows of the data-frame
The tail() function will show you the last few rows of the data-frame
The summary() function will give you an overview of the data-frame. What it gives you depends on the type of variable. For numeric variables, it will give you the minimum, maximum, mean, median and quartiles.


Action: Insert a new code chunk and use head(), tail() and summary() to get an overview of the data. Give it a go. If you’re stuck, have a look at the Code below.







TipCode





head(study.two.gen)
tail(study.two.gen)
summary(study.two.gen)



Questions Step 3

Data from how many participants does the data file contain?
What is the maximum age that was recorded for participants in this sample?
On average, are participants in this sample more accurate when tested on their understanding, or when self-rating their understanding of written health information?



Step 4: Draw histograms to examine the distributions of variables
Lets look at the distributions of mean.acc, mean.self and AGE.

Action: Insert a new code chunk and use ggplot() with geom_histogram() to look at the distributions of mean.acc, mean.self and age.







NoteHint





Use ggplot() with geom_histogram().
When we create a plot, we take things step-by-step.
ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = mean.acc)) + 
  geom_histogram()
These are the steps, set out one at a time:

ggplot(...) you tell R you want to make a plot using the ggplot() function
ggplot(data = study.two.gen ...) you tell R you want to make a plot with the study.two.gen data
ggplot(..., aes(x = mean.acc)) you tell R that you want to make a plot with the variable mean.acc – here, you specify the aesthetic mapping, x = mean.acc
ggplot(...) + geom_histogram() you tell R you want to plot values of mean.acc as a histogram

Notice that the code works the same whether we have the different bits of code on the same line or in a series of lines.



Questions Step 4
What do you conclude from the histograms in terms of distribution? Do the variables follow a normal distribution or are they skewed?

For the variable mean.acc?
For the variable mean.self?
For the variable AGE?



Step 5: Practice editing the appearance of a histogram plot step-by-step

Action 0.: In a new code chunk, use ggplot() with geom_histogram() to look at the distribution of SHIPLEY.

We are going to revise editing:

The appearance of the bars using binwidth.
The colour of the background using theme_bw().
The appearance of the labels using `labs().
Setting the x-axis limits to reflect the full range of possible scores on the x-axis variable.
Adding annotation – here, a vertical line – indicating the sample average for a variable.


Action 1. Edit the appearance of the bars by specifying a binwidth value.







TipCode





ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = SHIPLEY)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)




Action 2. Then add an edit to the appearance of the background using theme_bw().







TipCode





ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = SHIPLEY)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  theme_bw()




Action 3. Then add an edit to the appearance of the labels using labs().







TipCode





ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = SHIPLEY)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Vocabulary (SHIPLEY)", y = "Frequency count")




Action 4. Now add an edit by setting the x-axis limits using x.lim().







TipCode





ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = SHIPLEY)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Vocabulary (SHIPLEY)", y = "Frequency count") +
  xlim(0,40)




Action 5. Then add an edit to draw a vertical line to show the mean value of the variable you are plotting..







TipCode





ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = SHIPLEY)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Vocabulary (SHIPLEY)", y = "frequency count") +
  xlim(0,40) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(study.two.gen$SHIPLEY), colour = "red", size = 1.5)





Step 6: Create scatterplots to examine the association between some variables
Now we are ready to build a scatterplot to visualise the relationship between some variables. Our research questions are:

What person attributes predict success in understanding health information?
Can people accurately evaluate whether they correctly understand written health information?

Create three scatterplots to visualise the relationship between (1.) the outcome mean.acc and (2.) each of three numeric potential predictor variables SHIPLEY, HLVA and AGE.

Action: Insert a new code chunk and use ggplot() with geom_point()) to create a scatterplot. In both research questions, mean.acc is the outcome variable, so lets put that on the y-axis. Make several plots, with a different variable on the y-axis each time. If you need more guidance on how to do this, look at the Hint below.







NoteHint






We are working with geom_point() and you need x and y aesthetic mappings.
The outcome variable mean.acc has to be mapped to the y-axis using ...y = ...

This is how the target scatterplot code works.
ggplot(data = data.set, aes(x = predictor.variable, y = outcome.variable)) +
  geom_point()
The plot code moves through the following steps:

ggplot(...) make a plot;
ggplot(data = data.set, ...) working with the data.set, using the name you gave the dataset you are working with;
ggplot(...aes(x = predictor.variable, y = outcome.variable)) using two aesthetic mappings


x = predictor.variable maps values of the predictor.variable (whatever it is called) to x-axis (horizontal, left to right) positions;
y = outcome.variable maps values of the outcome.variable(whatever it is called) to y-axis (vertical, bottom to top) positions;


geom_point() show the mappings as points.






Step 7: Edit the appearance of each plot step-by-step






Tip



You may want to use the same plot appearance choices for all plots. Producing plots with a consistent appearance will make it easier for your audience to read your plots.








Tip



You can find more information about all the different parts of ggplot() in the ggplot() cheatsheet



Action 1. First, edit the appearance of the points using alpha, size, shape, and colour.







TipCode





Check out the example code for each of the scatterplots.

Notice what changes and what stays the same.

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = SHIPLEY, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = HLVA, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = AGE, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')




Action 2. Then edit the colour of the background using theme_bw().







TipCode





Check out the example code for each of the scatterplots.

Notice what changes and what stays the same.

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = SHIPLEY, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')   +
  theme_bw()

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = HLVA, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')   +
  theme_bw()

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = AGE, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')   +
  theme_bw()




Action 3. Then edit the appearance of the labels using labs().







TipCode





Check out the example code for each of the scatterplots.

Notice what changes and what stays the same.

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = SHIPLEY, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')   +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Vocabulary (SHIPLEY)", y = "Mean accuracy")

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = HLVA, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')   +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Health Literacy Test Score", y = "Mean accuracy")

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = AGE, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')   +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Age (Years)", y = "Mean accuracy")




Action 4. Then set the x-axis and y-axis limits to the minimum-maximum ranges of the variables you are plotting.

You can set axis limits by adding the xlim() and ylim() function calls to the chunk of code you have written to produce each plot.

The task, here, is to work out what numeric values you should enter inside xlim() or ylim().
The code works if you enter values like this: xlim(minimum, maximum) and ylim(minimum, maximum).
Where minimum, maximum are the numbers representing the smallest possible (minimum) and largest possible (maximum) value for each variable.







NoteHint






For these plots the y-axis limits will be the same because the outcome stays the same.
But the x-axis limits will be different for each different predictor variable.
Check out the information in the summary() you got of the dataset.
The minimum values for the variables will often (not always) be 0 e.g. if you are looking at data from ability tests and people who do the tests can get 0 (because none of their responses are correct). However, if you are looking at e.g. ratings data then the minimim value could be 1 (e.g. because people are asked to rate something on a scale from 1-9).
The maximum values for the variables is not necessarily the largest value recorded for that variable in the sample data-set you are working with (e.g., because nobody in your sample got all test questions correct). Thus, you need to use information about measurement design as summarised in Step 3.










TipCode





Check out the example code for each of the scatterplots.

Notice what changes and what stays the same.

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = SHIPLEY, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')   +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Vocabulary (SHIPLEY)", y = "Mean accuracy") +
  xlim(0, 40) + ylim(0, 1)

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = HLVA, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')   +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Health Literacy Test Score", y = "Mean accuracy") +
  xlim(0, 16) + ylim(0, 1)

ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = AGE, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')   +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Age (Years)", y = "Mean accuracy") +
  xlim(0, 80) + ylim(0, 1)





Step 8: Examine the correlations between the outcome variable and predictor variables
One of our research questions is:

What person attributes predict success in understanding?


Action: Examine the correlations between the outcome variable and predictor variables by running three separate correlations: 1. between mean accuracy and SHIPLEY; 2. between mean accuracy and HLVA; 3. between mean accuracy and AGE. Make sure to use ‘Bonferroni’ to adjust for conducting multiple correlations.







NoteHint





Use the correlation() function we used in earlier week. You need to specify the following information inside the correlation() function:

data: data = your.data
variables: select = c(“variable1”, “variable2”)
method = “pearson” or “spearman”
p_adjust = “none” or “Bonferroni”










TipCode





correlation(study.two.gen,
            select = c("SHIPLEY", "mean.acc"),
            method = "pearson",
            p_adjust = "bonferroni")

correlation(study.two.gen,
            select = c("HLVA", "mean.acc"),
            method = "pearson",
            p_adjust = "bonferroni")

correlation(study.two.gen,
            select = c("AGE", "mean.acc"),
            method = "pearson",
            p_adjust = "bonferroni")



Questions Step 8 Now use the results from the correlations to answer the following questions:

What is r, the coefficient for the correlation between mean.acc and SHIPLEY?
Is the correlation between mean.acc and HLVA significant?
What are the values for t and p for the significance test for the correlation between mean.acc and AGE?
For which pair of outcome-predictor variables is the correlation the largest?
What is the sign or direction of each of the correlations?



Step 9: Examine the relation between outcome mean accuracy (mean.acc) and each of the potential predictors: SHIPLEY, HLVA and AGE using the linear model






Important



The research question we are focussing on today is:

What person attributes predict success in understanding health information?




Action: In a new code chunk, write code to examine the relation between outcome mean accuracy (mean.acc) and each of the predictors: SHIPLEY, HLVA and AGE using the lm() function. Note that you need to run three separate lm() analyses: 1. with mean accuracy as the outcome and SHIPLEY as the predictor; 2. with mean accuracy as the outcome and HLVA as the predictor; 3. with mean accuracy as the outcome and AGE as the predictor. Use the information in the ‘Hint’ to help you. Try to write the code yourself. Compare the code you’ve written to the code snippet below.







NoteHow does the lm() function work?



You need to use lm() to do the analyses.

Be careful to identify the outcome and predictor variables correctly.
Remember that analysis code is arranged like this:

lm(outcome.variable ~ predictor.variable, data = data.set)
With:

lm() asking R to do the linear model analysis;
outcome.variable ~ ... specified on the left of the ~;
the predictor.variable ~ ... specified on the right of the ~;
and data.set identifying to R what dataset you are working with.

Notice that R has a general formula syntax:
outcome ~ predictor *or* y ~ x

and uses the same format across a number of different functions;
each time, the left of the tilde symbol ~ is some output or outcome;
and the right of the tilde ~ is some input or predictor or set of predictors.









TipCode





Check out the example code for each of the models.
model.1 <- lm(mean.acc ~ SHIPLEY, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.1)

model.2 <- lm(mean.acc ~ HLVA, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.2)

model.3 <- lm(mean.acc ~ AGE, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.3)



Questions Step 8

What is r, the coefficient for the correlation between mean.acc and SHIPLEY?
Is the correlation between mean.acc and HLVA significant?
What are the values for t and p for the significance test for the correlation between mean.acc and AGE?
For which pair of outcome-predictor variables is the correlation the largest?
What is the sign or direction of each of the correlations?



Step 10: Use a model we have fitted to plot model predictions
We can use the model we have just fitted to plot the model predictions. We are going to draw a scatterplot and add a line. The line will show the model predictions, given the model intercept and effect coefficient estimates.






NoteHint





You can see reference information here:
https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_abline.html




Action 1: In a new code chunk, first fit a model and get the summary: model the relationship between mean.acc and HLVA. Make a note of the following information from the model summary so you can use it next: the coefficient estimate for the intercept and the coefficient estimate for the slope of HLVA.







NoteHint





Use the lm() function, like you did in Step 9.









TipCode





model <- lm(mean.acc ~ HLVA, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model)




Action 2: Then, draw a prediction plot, using the geom_point() to draw a scatterplot and using the geom_abline() function to draw the prediction line representing the association between this outcome and predictor. Check first if you can write the code you need to produce the prediction plot. Then have a look at the code example: compare it to the code you wrote.







TipCode





ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = HLVA, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square')   +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0.522016, slope = 0.026207, 
              colour = "red", linewidth = 1.5) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "HLVA", y = "mean accuracy") +
  xlim(0, 15) + ylim(0, 1)

You will build the study on the Gorilla platform. Follow the instructions on the project page in the section Building the questionnaire study on Gorilla here.

Answers





Lab activity 1:
Questions Step 3

Data from how many participants does the data file contain?
What is the maximum age that was recorded for participants in this sample?
On average, how accurate are participants when tested on their understanding of written health information?







NoteQuestions Step 3: Answer






The data-frame has 172 rows, the variable participant_ID also is 172 items long. Both of these pieces of information suggest that there are 172 participants in the sample.
76
The mean for mean.acc (measured understanding) is .7679.




Questions Step 4
What do you conclude from the histograms in terms of distribution? Do the variables follow a normal distribution or are they skewed?

For the variable mean.acc?
For the variable mean.self?
For the variable AGE?







NoteQuestions Step 4: Answer






The variable mean.acc looks somewhat, but not massively, left-skewed (this is also referred to as negative skew). The long tail stretches out to the left. Most values cluster at the high end, with a few unusually low values dragging the tail out. The mean gets pulled down, so it sits to the left of the median (mean < median).
The distribution of mean.self is similarly left-skewed to that of mean.acc.
The variable AGE shows substantial right-skew. The long tail stretches out to the right. Most values cluster at the low end (with most participants being at the younger end), with a few unusually high values pulling the tail out. The mean gets dragged up, so it sits to the right of the median (mean > median).

A quick way to remember: The skew is named for the direction of the tail, not where the bulk of the data sits. The “hump” goes the opposite way to the label.



Questions Step 8

What is r, the coefficient for the correlation between mean.acc and SHIPLEY?
Is the correlation between mean.acc and HLVA significant?
What are the values for t and p for the significance test for the correlation between mean.acc and AGE?
For which pair of outcome-predictor variables is the correlation the largest?
What is the sign or direction of each of the correlations?







NoteQuestions Step 8: Answers






r = 0.47
Yes r is significant, because the value is p < .05.
t = 0.30, p = 0.764
The correlation is the largest between mean.acc and HLVA.
All the correlations are positive.




Questions Step 9

What is the estimate for the coefficient of the effect of the predictor HLVA on mean.acc?
Is the effect significant?
What are the values for t and p for the significance test for the coefficient?
How would you describe in words the shape or direction of the association between HLVA and mean.acc?
How how would you describe the relations apparent between the predictor and outcome in all three models?







NoteQuestions Step 9: Answers






0.026207
It is significant, p < .05
t = 7.529, p = 2.87e-12
The slope coefficient – and a scatterplot (draw it) – suggest that as HLVA scores increase so also do mean accuracy scores.

TipHow does filter() work?



The filter() function allows you to select specific rows from a data frame based on one or more conditions.
For example, imagine we have a dataset containing information about participants in a psychology study, including their age and gender. We might want to select only participants who are over 18 years old.
We can do this using:
filter(data, age > 18)
Here: - data is the name of our data frame. - age > 18 is the condition we want to apply. - note these two bits of information are separated within the function by a comma. - only rows where the condition is TRUE are kept.
We can also apply multiple conditions. For example, to select participants who are over 18 and identify as a woman:
filter(data, age > 18, gender == "Woman")
When we provide multiple conditions separated by commas, filter() keeps only rows that satisfy all of the conditions.

We can also use & (AND) and | (OR) to combine conditions.
For example:
filter(data, age >= 18 & age <= 30)
This selects participants aged between 18 and 30 (inclusive).

Use the function ggplot(). Start by writing ggplot() on the next line of the code chunk. Inside the ggplot() function, we need to tell R which data-frame (data=) and which variables to use (mapping=aes(x= , y= ))).
Then, we need to tell R what type of plot we want. We do this by adding a + to the line on which you’ve written ggplot(), then on the next line you add a ‘geometric object’, in this case geom_point().
We also want to add a line of best fit. This will give you a basic scatterplot. Revisit the lab activity code from week 1 to remind yourself how to change any of the features (such as the colour, the background, add titles to the axes etc.).



Many of the participants gave the same rating and read the same number of books, so their points sit exactly on top of each other. geom_jitter() fixes this by moving each point a tiny random amount, so overlapping points spread out and you can see how many there are.






TipHow does geom_jitter() work?



geom_jitter() moves each point a tiny random amount, so overlapping points spread out and you can see how many there are.
You can tell R how to jitter the data points:

width = 0.1 is the largest random nudge to the left or right. Ratings are whole numbers, so a point at 3 is moved to somewhere between 2.9 and 3.1. This is small enough that the five vertical stripes stay clearly separate.
height = 0 means the points are not moved up or down. The number of books is a real count, so nudging points vertically would make the plot show values that aren’t in the data.
alpha = 0.6 makes the points partly transparent (0 is invisible and 1 is solid). Where points overlap, the colour becomes darker, which gives a second clue about where the data are concentrated.

Jittering only changes how the plot looks. The data and the correlation are not affected.



Action: Instead of using geom_point() in the scatterplot, try geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, alpha = 0.6).

f. b and c All variables in b anc c are continuous. Dog breed and gender are categorical.





Question 2: Revision and exam marks
Forty students reported how many hours per week they spent revising and then sat an exam.


Look at the two histograms only. Does any student look unusual? Note anything you see.
Now look at the scatterplot. Which students do not fit the overall pattern? Describe each one, giving their approximate revision hours and exam mark.
Why can the scatterplot reveal something the histograms cannot?
Before running any analysis, what should you check about these students? Give two possible explanations for their scores.
If you calculated Pearson’s r for all 40 students, and then again without these students, would r get higher, lower or stay the same? Explain your reasoning.







NoteQuestion 2: Answer





a. Nothing clearly wrong. There are isolated bars at the ends of both histograms (about 5 and 25 hours; about 35 and 88 per cent), but each value is plausible on its own and nothing says that those bars belong to the same students.
b. Two students.

Participant 7: about 5 hours of revision but a mark of about 88%, much higher than the pattern predicts.
Participant 23: about 25 hours of revision but a mark of about 35%, much lower than the pattern predicts.

Both go against the positive trend shown by the other students.
c. The histograms show each variable on its own, and both students have values that are unusual but not impossible for each variable. They are only unusual in combination, which can only be seen when the two variables are plotted together.
d. Check for data-entry errors, such as typos, swapped or mismatched IDs, and misread marks. Other possibilities are a genuine but atypical participant (for example, prior knowledge from an earlier course, illness on the exam day, or a resit student) and a misunderstanding of the question about revision. The key message is to investigate and document, and not to delete cases just because they make the result awkward.
e. r would get higher. It looks like there may be a strong positive relationship without participants 7 and 23. I’d estimate r to be between .55 and .70. With the two students included, r is likely to be smaller as their datapoints go against the pattern of the rest of the sample.
Link to the lecture: in the simulation, a few participants who were extreme on both measures made about 20% of samples significant when there was no real relationship. Here the same kind of case has the opposite effect, masking a real relationship.





Question 3: Arousal and task performance
Sixty participants completed a memory task. Before the task, each was given a score for how aroused (alert and activated) they felt.


Describe the relationship between arousal and performance in words.
Look at the histograms. Do they suggest any problem with using Pearson’s r?
Without calculating anything, would you expect Pearson’s r to be strong and positive, strong and negative, or close to zero? Explain why.
Which assumption is violated here? Would switching to Spearman’s rho solve the problem? Why or why not?
What does this example tell you about reporting a correlation coefficient without looking at the scatterplot?







NoteQuestion 3: Answer





a. An inverted U. Performance is lowest at very low and very high arousal, and highest at moderate arousal (around 40 to 60).
b. Not really. The arousal histogram is roughly symmetrical, and the performance histogram has a slight tail towards low scores. Neither shows the curve.
c. Close to zero. The positive trend on the left of the plot cancels out the negative trend on the right.
d. Linearity. Spearman’s rho will not help, because the relationship is not monotonic: it rises and then falls.
e. A coefficient alone can hide a strong relationship. Always plot the data first. A correlation near zero means “no linear relationship”, not “no relationship”.





Question 4: Age and vocabulary
Eighty children aged between 6 and 16 took a vocabulary test.


Compare the spread of vocabulary scores for children aged about 7 to 8 with those aged about 13 to 15. Give approximate ranges for each group.
Which assumption is violated? Name it and describe what is wrong in your own words.
Could you have spotted this problem from the two histograms alone? Explain.
Why might this problem affect the p-value for Pearson’s r?
The spread of vocabulary scores grows roughly in proportion to the average score. Suggest one thing you could try.







NoteQuestion 4: Answer





a. Around 7 to 8 years, scores are roughly 1,200 to 2,000 words (a range of about 800). Around 13 to 15 years, they are roughly 2,900 to 5,800 (a range of nearly 3,000). The spread is clearly larger for older children.
b. Homoscedasticity (equal spread). The spread of Y is not constant across X: the scatter fans out as age increases.
c. No. Both histograms look reasonably bell-shaped, and nothing about them suggests a problem. The unequal spread is a feature of the relationship, which only the scatterplot shows.
d. Because Pearson’s r assumes the spread is similar at every value of X. When it isn’t, the p-value can be inaccurate. In the lecture simulation, funnel-shaped data produced about twice as many false positives as expected when there was no real relationship.
e. Spearman’s rho is an option, but it only partly helps with unequal spread. Analysing age groups separately is a possibility. There are other options you’ll learn about later (using regression or log-transforming the data).





Question 5: Reaction time and social media use
Eighty participants completed a reaction-time task and reported how many hours per week they spend on social media. Figure 4a shows the raw data.



Figure 5a. Raw data.



Describe the shape of each histogram.
Does the scatterplot look like an oval, bell-shaped cloud? Which assumption(s) appear to be violated?
In the lecture simulations, what happened to the false-positive rate when variables were skewed but unrelated? What would you still want to check in the scatterplot?

Figure 4b shows the same data after taking the natural log of both variables. Transforming the the data in this way is common approach for heavily skewed data.



Figure 5b. The same data on a log scale.



What has changed? Has the transformation solved every problem?
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of log-transforming the data.







NoteQuestion 5: Answer





a. Both are strongly right-skewed. Reaction time peaks around 300 to 400 ms with a long tail to about 1,700 ms. Social media use peaks at under 10 hours per week with a long tail to about 140 hours.
b. No. Most points are crowded at the lower left, with a few extreme points scattered to the right and above. The main problem is non-normality of both variables (skew), and the few extreme points could have a large influence on r.
c. When skewed variables were independent, the false-positive rate stayed at about 5%, so the test was robust to skew. However, you should still check the scatterplot for extreme points that might have a large influence, and for any curvature.
d. Both histograms are more symmetrical, and the scatterplot is a more evenly spread cloud, with no extreme points dominating. It isn’t perfect: reaction time is still slightly right-skewed after the log transform.
e. Advantage: it keeps all the information in the data, and often makes proportional relationships linear and spreads even. It is also common for variables like reaction times. Disadvantage: results are on a log scale, so they are harder to interpret and to explain, and it can’t be used for zero or negative values without adjustment.






Lab activity 3:
Questions Step 2 a. How many participants does the data frame data_thirty contain? b. How many degrees of freedom would you expect to see in the output if you were to run a correlation analysis with the variables vocabulary and experience using the data_thirty data frame?
::: {.callout-note title=“Questions Step 3: Answers icon=”false” collapse=“true”} a. The data_thirty data frame contains data from 30 participants. We can see this from the number of rows (or obs.) it has. b. The degrees of freedom for a correlation analysis are determined by the sample size (N) minus 2. If all participants had complete data, we would expect the degrees of freedom to be 30-2 = 28. :::
Questions Step 3 a. How many data points are missing? b. How many participants have complete data? c. How many degrees of freedom are reported in the output from the correlation analysis. Explain how that number is derived. Does it match what you expected to see based on the number of participants?






NoteQuestions Step 4: Answers






There are 6 missing data points.
The data frame contains 25 participants who have complete data.
The degrees of freedom reported in the output from the correlation analysis is 23. Because only 25 participants have complete data and correlation analysis requires participants to contribute a data point on each variable, the other participants are dropped from the analysis. This leaves us with N=25-2 = 23 degrees of freedom.






Lab activity 4:
Questions Step 3 a. Looking at the line of best fit in the first scatterplot (which included the participants with outlier values), how would you describe the relationship between revision hours and exam mark? b. What do you estimate the value of the correlation coefficient to be? c. Looking at the line of best fit in the second scatterplot (without the participants with outlier values), how would you describe the relationship between revision hours and exam mark now? d. What do you estimate the value of the correlation coefficient to be now?






NoteQuestions Step 3: Answers






The line of best fit is a horizontal line, suggesting there is no relationship between revision hours and exam mark.
The correlation coefficient is likely around 0.
The line of best fit suggest a positive relationship between revision hours and exam mark. People who spent more hours revising, performed better in the exam.
As the datapoints are relatively close to the line, the correlation coefficient is likely to between .60 and .70.




Questions Step 4 a. What is r for the relationship between revision hours and exam mark when using the data that includes participants with outlier values? Is it significant? b. What is r for the relationship between revision hours and exam mark when using the data that does not include participants with outlier values? Is it significant?






NoteQuestions Step 4: Answers






Using the full data set we found no significant correlation between weekly revision hours and exam marks, r(38) = .05, p = .757.
After removing two participants, there was a strong positive correlation between weekly revision hours and exam marks, r(36) = .67, p < .001. People who revised for more hours, scored higher on the exam.






Lab activity 5:
Questions Step 3 a. What is the value for Pearson’s r, is it significant? b. What is the value for Spearman’s rho, is it significant? c. What is the correct correlation coefficient to use. Explain why.






NoteQuestions Step 3: Answers






Pearson: r(58) = .23, p = .079, which is not significant.
Spearman: rho(58) = .60, p < .001, which is significant.
The main reason is that one variable (reading_enjoyment) is ordinal. A single rating item has ordered categories, but nobody can say that the step from 1 to 2 equals the step from 4 to 5. Pearson’s r assumes equal intervals. In the scatterplot, the points fall in five vertical stripes instead of a cloud, which is a sign of ordinal data. Additionally, the other variable (books_read) is a skewed count. Most people read a handful of books, but two heavy readers (48 and 56 books) are far from everyone else. Those two sit at middling enjoyment ratings, so they pull a straight line away from the real trend. Because Spearman’s rho is based on ranks, it is less affected by those values and the overall trend is captured more accurately.

Pre-lab activities
The lecture material is designed to deliver important ideas and procedures for learning about psychological science and analysis. Pre-lab material is then designed to help consolidate this learning, or enhance, expand and apply it in ways that set the scene for the lab session activity. We want to prepare you to be ready to go in the session itself and make the most of your time there.
These short activities will help you connect Week 2’s emphasis on data visualisation to this week’s work with understanding relationships between two numerical variables.

Pre-lab activity 1: Why visualise data? Anscombe’s quartet
Last week, we considered the importance of visualising your data and not to just rely on the summary numbers. These measures of central tendency (e.g., mean, median, mode) are also referred to as ‘descriptive statistics’ or ‘summary statistics’. This is because we use them to summarise and describe our data, but we do not use them to make any inferences about our data.
Anscombe’s quartet (1973) showed that four different sets of bivariate data (where X and Y are both recorded for each participant) with very similar summary statistics (including means, variances and Pearson correlation coefficients) can look very different when plotted. You can read more about this and explore the four plots here.
Look closely at the plots. Which one looks approximately linear? Which shows a curved pattern? Where does a single unusual observation have a particularly strong influence?






NoteTakeaway



A correlation coefficient is useful, but looking at a scatterplot helps us spot features that one number cannot show.




Pre-lab activity 2: Visualising correlations interactively
Have a look at this visualisation of correlations by Kristoffer Magnusson.
After having read the relevant sections of Howell (2017) Chapter 9 (see under Reading), use this visualisation page to visually replicate the scatterplots in Figures 9.1 and 9.2 - use a sample of 100. After that, visually replicate the scatterplots in Figure 9.3.
Each time you change the correlation, pay attention to the shared variance (the overlap between the two variables, based on R²) and see how this changes with the changing level of relationship between the two variables. The greater the shared variance, the stronger the relationship.
Also, try setting the correlation to r = .5 and then moving a single dot to see how one data point, a potential outlier, can change the stated correlation value between two variables.


Pre-lab activity 3: Guess the correlation
Try this online app on guessing the correlation.
This allows you to see how accurately you can estimate r (correlation strengths) from a scatterplot. Click on “Track Performance” first so you can keep an overview of your overall bias to underestimate or overestimate the strength of a correlation.
Is this all just a bit of fun? Well, yes, because stats is actually fun, and no, because it serves a purpose of helping you determine if the correlations you see in your own data are real, and to help you see if correlations in published research match with what you are being told. As you will have seen from the above examples, one data point can lead to a misleading relationship and even what might be considered a medium to strong relationship may actually have only limited relevance in the real world. It is our responsibility as psychological scientists to interpret our findings appropriately and to not overstate our results. We will think more about this in the lab this week.

Suppose it was observed that there is a correlation of r = -.81 between a driver’s age and the cost of car insurance. This correlation would mean that, in general, older people pay more for car insurance.







NoteAnswer





FALSE Explanation: The correlation coefficient is negative and therefore infers a negative correlation. As such, older people pay less for car insurance: as age increases, car insurance costs decrease.




Suppose that there is a correlation of r = .87 between the length of time a person is in prison and the amount of aggression the person displays on a psychological inventory administered at release. This means that spending a longer amount of time in prison causes people to become more aggressive.







NoteAnswer





FALSE Explanation: This is a bit of trick question as it has the sneaky ‘cause’ word in. The correlation coefficient is a positive number, suggesting a positive relationship between length of time in prison and aggression. However, causation cannot be inferred from correlation and therefore we cannot know whether time spent in prison CAUSES aggression, and rather we suggest a relationship between the two: as length of time in prison increases, aggression increases.




A significant correlation was found between having great hair and performance in research methods and stats labs. The correlation coefficient was .7. How much variance in research methods and stats lab performance can the ‘greatness’ of your hair explain?







NoteAnswer





c 49% The ‘coefficient of determination’ or ‘R-squared’ tells us the proportion or variance in one variable that can be predicted if we know the other variable. We can determine this by squaring the r. Therefore, .72 = .49, R2 = .49.

Lab activities

Lab activity 1: Reading in data and creating a plot

Background
We’ve all been there: you may be trying to focus on a lecture, but a thought on what you would like to have for lunch pops into your mind. Mind wandering describes the common experience of one’s thoughts drifting away from the task at hand towards self-generated thoughts and feelings (Smallwood & Schooler, 2006). Today, we’ll work with some publicly available data from a research project on mind wandering. Anna Schubert and colleagues (Schubert et al., 2024) conducted a study in which they created a 12-item questionnaire that measures how often your mind wanders without meaning to, how often you let it wander on purpose, and how aware you are when it happens. You can have a look at the questionnaire here.


Aims of the activity
We are going to:

Download the files
Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio
Read in the data
Build a plot







TipWatch the ‘How to’ lecture



If you haven’t done so already, this is a good time to watch the ‘How to’ video (here Section 1.3) on ‘How to build a plot’.




Step 1: Download the files
To complete this lab activity you will need two files:

We’ll work with an example script called 4141_wk1_lab_act1.qmd. This is a Quarto document.
We need a data file called data_bmw3.csv. This is a file that contains the responses of the participants in one of the studies reported on in the paper by Schubert et al. (2024). It is a file of the type .csv. This means that individual bits of data are separated by comma’s. We’ll often use .csv files.

You can download the files here: 4141_wk1_lab.zip. Usually they will be saved in your ‘Downloads’ folder.
Next, upload the zip-folder as it is to your Files space on the R-server (bottom right quadrant; no need to extract the files first).
Finally, open the example script by clicking on the file called 4141_wk1_lab_act1.qmd in the Files space on the R-server.


Steps 2, 3 and 4
For steps 2, 3 and 4, you’ll be working in RStudio.
References
Schubert, A.-L., Frischkorn, G. T., Sadus, K., Welhaf, M. S., Kane, M. J., & Rummel, J. (2024). The brief mind wandering three-factor scale (BMW-3). Behavior Research Methods, 56(8), 8720-8744. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-024-02500-6
