1. What you are being asked to do?
This term your group designed and ran a study on whether mind wandering is related to screen time. Your task now is to write an individual research report about that study. The report should read like a short journal article: it tells the story of one question, from the reason for asking it, through how you tested it, to what you found and what it means.
You will use the data your group collected, but the analysis and the writing are your own work.






WarningKey information



What do you need to do? Analyse the data from the PSYC4141 research project and write up the results in a research report no longer than 1500 words, plus a 150 word abstract.
When is the deadline? Friday of Week 10 at 12 noon (Friday 11th December 2026)
How do you submit your coursework? You need to submit 2 documents: 1) Submit your report as a Quarto document (.qmd) and your Feedback title sheet as a Word document (.docx) via the submission space on the PSYC4141 Moodle page.
How does the report contribute to your module mark? The mark for the report accounts for 35% of your module mark.








ImportantAcademic integrity



PSYC4141 is a RED module. This means that you must not use Gen AI tools for any aspect of your work. You will need to confirm that you have not used AI to generate or edit your thoughts/content/words using the AI Transparency Sheet that is part of the Feedback Title sheet. For those students with an ILSP that permits the use of AI tools, you will need to indicate that you have used them and complete an AI transparency appendix as outlined for AMBER and GREEN modules.
Please refer to the general Assessment Guidance on Moodle including the Lancaster University Department of Psychology Academic Integrity Student Guide for further details.

section: 2. What the report is about: A chain of alignment
text:
2. What the report is about: A chain of alignment
The most important thing we are looking for is not a surprising result. It is a report in which every part connects to the next one. Think of it as a chain:









Introduction
Method
Results
Discussion




idea → research question → hypothesis
methods
results
critical evaluation → take-home message




Your introduction explains the idea behind the study and why it matters, leads the reader to your research question, and states your hypothesis: a specific, testable prediction that answers that question.
Your method describes how you tested that hypothesis, and you can justify the choices you made.
Your results report the analysis that tests the hypothesis, and nothing that wanders off it.
Your discussion first evaluates your study critically (who took part, how things were measured, what limits the conclusions), then gives a take-home message that answers the research question using only what the results can support.

Your abstract sits at the start but is written last. It is the whole chain in miniature: a sentence or two on each link, in the same order. If you cannot write it, a link in your report is probably missing.
If one link is weak (for example, a hypothesis that your measures cannot test, or a conclusion that goes beyond your data), the whole report suffers, however well the rest is written. A modest study with a tight chain will score better than an ambitious one with gaps.

title: 13. The Report page
text:
3. What your report should contain
Your report follows the structure of a short empirical article:







Section
What it does




Title
Tells the reader what the study is about


Abstract
Summarises the whole study in a short paragraph, following the same chain as the report


Introduction
Gives the rationale for the study, ends with your research question and hypothesis


Method
Describes participants, measures, procedure and ethics so another researcher could repeat the study


Results
Reports the correlation analysis, with a table or figure, and states whether the hypothesis was supported


Discussion
Interprets the result, considers who took part and what limits the conclusions, and ends with a clear take-home message


References
Lists every source you cite



Detailed guidance on each section, including why APA asks for things to be done in a particular way, is in the Writing Guide in Section 5.1. The Marking Criteria in Section 4 below show how the report will be marked.

The analysis
You will test your hypothesis using correlation. You will run this analysis yourself in R, inside your Quarto document. You will use the group dataset, but you must run, interpret and report the analysis yourself.


The Quarto document
You submit a single Quarto document (.qmd). It contains your report text and the code that produces your analysis, so that anyone can see exactly how your numbers were produced.
You can use this Quarto template to get started.

You write the code for your analysis yourself, using what you have learned in previous weeks. You do not need to learn advanced Quarto features.
You type the numbers into your text yourself, reading them from your output. The values you report must come from your output, but you round them as APA requires (the Writing Guidance explains how), so you will not copy every decimal place.
Each code block in your document must run without errors.



Your study and your data
Your group:

chose how to measure mind wandering and screen time, and submitted a pre-registration with your research question, hypotheses and measures;
collected data from about 50 adult participants (recruited from your own networks) through Gorilla.

Your report should be based on your group’s pre-registration, plus the changes you made based on the feedback you received. You may reuse wording from your pre-registration.
The data are shared within your group, and it does not matter if the wording you take from your pre-registration overlaps with that of other students in your group. Everything else, including your analysis and how you explain and interpret your results, must be your own work. Reports that are copied from each other beyond this will be treated as an academic integrity issue.


Word count and formatting

The limit is 1500 words. This excludes the title, abstract, figures, tables and reference list. In-text citation are included in the word count. The abstract should be no longer than 150 words.
Follow APA 7 for headings, in-text citations, the reference list, and the presentation of statistics, tables and figures.



Before you submit, check that:

each part of your report follows from the part before it;
your hypothesis can be tested with the measures you used;
the numbers in your text come from your output and are rounded and formatted as APA requires;
your conclusions do not go further than your data allow;
each code block in your Quarto document runs without errors;
you are within the word limit and have cited and referenced in APA style.

title: 13. The Report page
text:
4. How is your report marked?
Your report is judged on six criteria. For each one, the marker chooses a category: Needs work, Acceptable, Good or Outstanding. Your feedback shows a grid with one tick per criterion, so you can see your profile at a glance, followed by comments on what went well and what to do next time. Your overall mark comes from that profile and the marker’s overall judgement (see Section 4.7 below).
Three things to know:

Alignment matters most. The criteria follow the chain from idea to take-home message, and one criterion looks at whether the chain holds across the whole report, including the abstract.
Your result does not decide your mark. A weak, zero or unexpected correlation can earn top marks if the report is aligned, honest and well evaluated. A significant result in a report with broken links cannot.
Use the grid before you submit. Read each criterion, choose the category you think your report reaches, and find the evidence for it in your own text.


Criterion 1 - Introduction: idea, research question and hypotheses







Category
What it looks like




Outstanding
Explains why the idea matters, using relevant sources, including a theory or mechanism that could explain why screen time and mind wandering might be associated. Narrows step by step to a research question. States both the null and the alternative hypothesis, which follow directly from that argument, name both variables and state the expected relationship.


Good
A clear rationale, question, and testable null and alternative hypotheses. The theory or mechanism is relevant but only partly linked to the hypotheses, or the step from rationale to hypotheses could be tighter.


Acceptable
The topic is introduced and a question is stated, but the rationale is general or descriptive, and any theory or mechanism is mentioned rather than explained. The hypotheses are vague, only one is stated, or they do not clearly follow.


Needs work
The rationale is missing or unclear, with no theory or mechanism. The question or hypotheses are missing, cannot be tested, or do not match the study.





Criterion 2 - Method







Category
What it looks like




Outstanding
Another researcher could repeat the study: participants (including the sample size and how they were recruited), measures, procedure and ethics are all clear. Each measure is plainly a measure of a variable in the hypotheses, with a reason for the choice.


Good
Complete and clear, including the sample size, with minor gaps. The link between measures and hypotheses is clear but the justification is thin.


Acceptable
Most information is there, but gaps would stop someone repeating the study, or the link between measures and hypotheses is left for the reader to work out.


Needs work
Key information is missing (such as the sample size), a measure does not match the hypotheses, or the description is too vague to allow replication.





Criterion 3 - Results







Category
What it looks like




Outstanding
Presents the data to the reader with descriptive statistics for each variable in the text or a table; a figure helps the reader see the pattern. The correlation analysis suits the data, with the checks taught in the module reported briefly. Statistics are reported correctly in APA format. States whether the null hypothesis is rejected or not rejected (never “accepted”) and what this means for the alternative hypothesis. The code runs and produces the reported numbers.


Good
Descriptive statistics and a table and/or figure are present, and the analysis is correct, with minor reporting slips. The table or figure could be clearer, or the decision about the null hypothesis is correct but briefly worded.


Acceptable
Descriptive statistics are incomplete, or the table and/or figure is missing or hard to follow. The analysis is broadly right, but with errors in reporting or interpretation, or the decision about the null hypothesis is unclear.


Needs work
Descriptive statistics are missing or incorrect. The analysis is inappropriate or conducted incorrectly, the numbers in the text do not match the output, there is no decision about the null hypothesis, or the code does not run.





Criterion 4 - Discussion: critical evaluation and take-home message







Category
What it looks like




Outstanding
Answers the research question first. Relates the finding to key findings in the literature, saying whether it fits them and what might explain any difference. Evaluates this study specifically: who took part and how they were recruited, how each concept was measured, and why a correlation cannot show cause. Explains how each point affects what can be concluded. Ends with a take-home message that goes no further than the data.


Good
Answers the question, relates the finding to the literature and evaluates the study sensibly, but the link to the literature is brief, some points are not linked back to the conclusion, or the take-home message is slightly broad.


Acceptable
Mostly restates the results, with little or no link to the literature. Limitations are generic (for example “small sample”) and not tied to this study’s conclusion. The take-home message is vague or overreaches.


Needs work
No real evaluation, no link to the literature, or conclusions the results do not support (for example, claiming screen time causes mind wandering).





Criterion 5 - Alignment across the report
This criterion is judged on the report as a whole, including the title and abstract.







Category
What it looks like




Outstanding
Each part follows from the one before: the question fits the idea, the hypotheses answer the question, the methods can test them, the results address them, and the discussion answers the question. The abstract mirrors this chain. A reader could sum up the study in one sentence.


Good
The chain holds, with one weak link (for example, a hypothesis that is slightly broader than the measures can test).


Acceptable
The chain is visible but has two or more weak links, or one clear mismatch between sections.


Needs work
Sections read as separate pieces. The hypotheses, measures, results and conclusion do not address the same question.





Criterion 6 - Scientific writing and APA







Category
What it looks like




Outstanding
APA 7 is applied accurately and consistently: heading levels and wording, in-text citations, the reference list, the formatting of numbers and statistics, and the numbering and titling of tables and figures. Writing is clear and concise, in a scientific style. The abstract is self-contained. Within the word limit.


Good
APA 7 is mostly accurate with a few inconsistencies. Writing is clear, with occasional wordiness or informality.


Acceptable
APA 7 is attempted but with repeated errors. Writing sometimes obscures the meaning. The abstract is missing a part of the story.


Needs work
APA 7 is largely absent. Writing makes the report hard to follow. Over the word limit, or no abstract.





From criteria to overall mark
The overall mark is a judgement guided by your profile, not an average. As a guide:







Grade
Typical profile




A (A+, A, A-)
Alignment is Outstanding, at least three other criteria are Outstanding, and none is below Good.


B (B+, B, B-)
Alignment is Good or better, most criteria are Good with some Outstanding, and none is below Acceptable.


C (C+, C, C-)
Mostly Acceptable and Good. Alignment is at least Acceptable.


D (D+, D, D-)
Mostly Acceptable, with some Needs work.


F (F1 to F4)
Mostly Needs work, or the hypotheses are not tested. F4 is reserved for no attempt made.



The plus or minus shows how securely the profile fits the grade. Use a plus when the profile sits at the top of the grade (for a B, for example, Alignment is Outstanding or several criteria are Outstanding), a plain letter for a typical fit, and a minus when the profile only just meets the grade (for a B, Alignment is only Good and one criterion is Acceptable).

title: 13. The Report page
text:
5. Further help and resources
Key sections: - See Section 5.1 for further guidance on each section. - See Section 3.2 to download the Quarto template. - See Section 4 for the marking criteria.






TipGetting started



To start planning the introduction for your research report. Your pre-registration, the feedback on it and your responses to that feedback together give you a strong starting point for your introduction. In the pre-registration you made decisions about your research question, hypotheses and measures. The feedback asked you to look closely at those decisions, and your responses show how you justified or changed them. That reasoning is the basis of the argument your introduction needs to make: why your study makes sense and why it is designed the way it is. You can complete this optional activity Building the rationale for your study to help you turn these notes into a plan.



Writing Guide
This guide takes you through your research report section by section. For each section it explains what the section is for, what to include, and why APA asks you to do things in a particular way. It uses the same criteria your report will be marked against, so you can use it to plan, draft and check your report.

The big idea: alignment
A research report is an argument. Each part leads into the next one, and the parts have to fit together. We call this alignment. It is the most important thing in your report, and it has its own marking criterion.








Link in the chain
The question it answers
Where it goes




Idea
What are we interested in, and why does it matter?
Introduction


Research question
What exactly are we asking?
Introduction


Hypotheses
What do we expect to find, and why?
Introduction


Method
How did we test it?
Method


Results
What did we find?
Results


Critical evaluation
How far can we trust and generalise this finding?
Discussion


Take-home message
So what does this mean?
Discussion



A quick test for alignment: a reader should be able to read just your hypotheses and your take-home message and see that they match. If your introduction promises something that your method doesn’t measure, or your discussion draws a conclusion your results don’t support, the chain is broken.






TipSuggested word budgets



Introduction ~450 · Method ~300 · Results ~250 · Discussion ~500. This is only a guide, so move words to where your argument needs them.




Title and abstract
Title. Say what you studied in one line, naming both variables, e.g. “Is daily screen time related to mind wandering in young adults?”. Avoid clever puns that hide the topic.
Abstract (about 150 words in a single paragraph, not counted in the word limit). This is a summary of the whole chain in miniature: one or two sentences each for the idea and why it matters, research question, hypotheses, method (including sample size and measures), main result (with the statistic), and take-home message. Write it last.
Tense: use the past tense for what you did and found (“We measured…”, “Screen time was positively correlated with…”). Use the present tense for your conclusion and what it means (“This suggests…”).






NoteWhy APA does it this way




Standing alone: most readers decide from the title and abstract whether to read on, and databases index them. They need to make sense on their own, so don’t include citations or abbreviations that are only explained later.
Tense: your study is finished, so what you did and found are completed events, which take the past tense. Your conclusion is a claim you are making now, so it takes the present tense. The same rule runs through the whole report.





Introduction
The introduction contains the first three links in the chain: idea → research question → hypotheses. Its job is to persuade the reader that your study is worth doing and is designed sensibly. In APA style the introduction has no heading, because the title does that job, so start writing straight after the abstract.
A good structure moves from broad to narrow:

Introduce the concepts. What is mind wandering? How is screen time defined and measured? Use the definitions that match the measures your group chose.
Explain why they might be related. Give a theory or mechanism. For example, how might heavy phone use shape attention, or how might a tendency to mind wander lead people to reach for their phone? Support this with sources.
Summarise what is already known. What have previous studies found? Where are the gaps or inconsistencies?
State your research question. It should follow logically from the gap.
State your hypotheses. Give both the null (H0) and the alternative (H1). Name both variables and say what relationship you expect. If you predict a direction (positive or negative), the introduction must explain why.

Tense: use the present tense for definitions, theories and established knowledge (“Mind wandering is…”, “Attention is a limited resource…”). Use the past tense for what specific earlier studies did and found (“Smith (2020) found…”). Use the past tense for your own hypotheses, because the study has already been carried out (“We hypothesised that…”).






TipStart from your pre-registration



You don’t need to start from a blank page. Your pre-registration, the feedback on it and your responses to the feedback already contain your research question, hypotheses and the reasons for your decisions. See Building the rationale for your study for an activity that turns these into a plan for your introduction.
Your pre-registration was written before you collected data, so it is in the future tense (“We will measure…”, “We predict…”). Change this to the past tense when you reuse it in your report.








NoteWhy APA does it this way




Present tense for ideas that are still true: a definition or theory isn’t tied to one moment, so it is written as currently true.
Past tense for specific studies: a particular study was carried out at a particular time, so its findings are reported as completed events. This also makes clear to the reader which claims come from one study and which are general knowledge.
Citations at the point of the claim: putting the citation right after the idea it supports shows the reader exactly where each claim comes from.









WarningCommon pitfalls




Describing lots of studies one by one without saying how they build to your question.
Hypotheses that appear out of nowhere, with no reason given for the predicted direction.
Introducing concepts or measures that never appear in your method.





Method
The method says how you tested your hypotheses. Write it in enough detail that someone else could repeat your study. Use the past tense and these subheadings:

Participants: the final sample size, how participants were recruited (e.g. an opportunity sample from your group’s social networks), any inclusion criteria, and key demographics (e.g. age range and mean, gender). If any participants were excluded, say how many and why.
Measures: how you measured mind wandering, screen time and any demographics. Name each questionnaire, cite it, and say how many items it has, what the response scale is and how scores were calculated (e.g. the mean of all items, with higher scores meaning more mind wandering). Say why each measure suits the variable in your hypotheses. If you used phone screen time data, explain exactly what was recorded and over what period. Use digits for scale points and scores, even below 10 (e.g. “a 5-point scale ranging from 1 = never to 5 = always”).
Procedure: what participants did, in order, and how long it took. Mention that the study ran online on Gorilla and had ethical approval, and say how ethical issues were handled (consent, the right to withdraw, debrief).







NoteWhy APA does it this way




Detail and subheadings: replication is how science checks its findings. A method section with clear subheadings lets readers find details quickly and judge whether the measures really capture the concepts from your introduction.
Past tense: the method is a record of what actually happened (“Participants completed…”). This is the main difference between your method and your pre-registration. The one exception is describing a questionnaire that still exists, which can be in the present tense (“The scale consists of 12 items…”).









TipHow to cite Gorilla?



To cite Gorilla in your research report, please link to the main website www.gorilla.sc. We also recommend stating the date window within which data was collected, so that someone reading the study could cross-reference this with their release notes. Make sure to include the reference below:
Anwyl-Irvine, A. L., Massonnié, J., Flitton, A., Kirkham, N., & Evershed, J. K. (2020). Gorilla in our midst: An online behavioral experiment builder. Behavior Research Methods, 52(1), 388–407. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-019-01237-x




Results
The results report what you found, without interpreting it. Interpretation goes in the discussion.

Descriptive statistics. First things first: you need to present the data to the reader. Report the means and standard deviations for both variables, rounded to two decimal places, in the text, or in a table if you have more than two variables (for example, because you looked at more than one aspect of mind wandering). Number every table and figure (Table 1, Figure 1) and refer to it by number in the text (e.g. “see Figure 1”). Put the number in bold, and the title in italics and title case, above the table or figure. Tables have no vertical lines, and figures need clearly labelled axes, with units.
The inferential test. Illustrate the main finding by including an appropriate figure. A scatterplot is ideal for a correlation. Say which test you used and why (e.g. a Pearson correlation, because both variables are continuous), and report the checks you were taught. Then report the result in APA format, with a 95% confidence interval, e.g. r(48) = .32, 95% CI [.05, .55], p = .023. Put your analysis code in code blocks before or alongside the text that reports it.
Link back to the hypotheses. State whether you reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis (never “accept” it), and what this means for your alternative hypothesis, e.g. “There was a weak, positive, statistically significant correlation between screen time and mind wandering, so the null hypothesis was rejected in favour of the alternative hypothesis.”

Tense: use the past tense for your findings (“Mind wandering was positively correlated with…”). Use the present tense when pointing the reader to a table or figure, because it is in front of them now (“Table 1 shows…”).






NoteWhy APA does it this way




Past tense for results: your results describe what happened in your sample, at the time you collected the data. Writing “was correlated” rather than “is correlated” also stops you claiming more than your data show.
Statistical symbols are in italics (M, SD, N, r, p) so they stand out from the text. N is the whole sample and n is part of it.
Spaces around =, < and > make statistics easier to read, just as spaces between words do.
Words or digits: small numbers read more naturally as words in a sentence. Digits are used wherever precision matters, such as data, measurements and scales, so readers can quickly spot and compare the values that carry your evidence.
Digits for all statistics: values such as M = 3.42 and r = .32 are always written in digits, however small. If a sentence would start with a number, rephrase it.
No leading zero for r and p (.32, not 0.32), because these values can never be greater than 1. Values that can be greater than 1 keep the zero (M = 0.85), so the missing zero tells the reader something.
Degrees of freedom go in brackets. For a correlation, df = N − 2. This lets readers check your sample size.
Rounding: r to two decimal places, p to three. For means and standard deviations for integer-scale data (e.g., surveys): one decimal, and two decimals for other means and SDs. Your output shows many more digits, but they suggest a precision your data don’t have.
Exact p values give more information than “p < .05”. Use p < .001 for very small values.
The confidence interval shows the range of plausible values for the true correlation, so readers can see how precise your estimate is, not just whether it is significant.

See the APA Style Guide - Numbers and Statistics for full guidance.








WarningYour code and your numbers must agree



Your Quarto document has to include the code for your descriptive statistics, your figure or table, and your correlation. Every number you write in the text must match what your code produces. Check them carefully before you submit.




Discussion
The discussion contains the last two links in the chain: critical evaluation → take-home message. It moves from narrow back to broad, so it mirrors your introduction.

Answer your research question first, in plain words and without repeating the statistics, and say whether the finding supports your hypothesis.
Relate it to the literature. Is it consistent with the studies and the mechanism from your introduction? If not, why might that be?
Critically evaluate. Focus on the issues that matter for your conclusions:

Who you recruited. How might a sample drawn from your own social networks affect the relationship you found and who it generalises to?
Measurement. How well do your measures capture the concepts? For example, how accurate is self-reported screen time?
Correlation is not causation. Could screen time affect mind wandering, mind wandering affect screen time, or could a third variable affect both?

For each limitation, explain how it affects your conclusion and suggest a specific way future research could address it.
Finish with a take-home message. What should the reader remember? It should answer your research question and match your hypotheses.

Tense: use the past tense when restating your findings and those of other studies (“We found…”, “Jones (2021) also reported…”). Use the present tense for interpretation, implications and your take-home message (“This suggests…”, “Future research should…”).






NoteWhy APA does it this way




Narrow to broad: the discussion mirrors the introduction, so the reader ends where they started, with the bigger question, and can see what your study has added.
Switching tense: the past tense marks what was observed, and the present tense marks what you are claiming it means. Keeping the two apart lets the reader see where your evidence ends and your interpretation begins, which is the core of critical evaluation.









WarningCommon pitfalls




A generic list of limitations (“the sample was small”) with no explanation of why it matters for this finding.
Causal language (“screen time causes mind wandering”) about a correlational study.
New results, or ideas that were never introduced, appearing only in the discussion.





References and APA style
Headings: use the headings in the template. Method, Results, Discussion and References are main headings (APA Level 1, written with #). Participants, Measures and Procedure are subheadings (APA Level 2, written with ##). Write headings in title case, and don’t add other main headings.
Citations in the text follow APA 7th edition:

One author: Smith (2020) found…, or … (Smith, 2020).
Two authors: Smith and Jones (2020) found…, or … (Smith & Jones, 2020). Use “and” in the sentence and “&” inside brackets.
Three or more authors: Smith et al. (2020) found…, or … (Smith et al., 2020).
Paraphrase rather than quote. Give a page number only for a direct quote.

Reference list: list every source in APA 7 format, in alphabetical order by the first author’s surname. Every source cited in the text must be in the reference list, and the other way round. APA uses a hanging indent, but you do not need to create one in your Quarto document. The pattern for a journal article is:
Author, A. A., & Author, B. B. (Year). Title of the article in sentence case. Name of the Journal in Title Case, volume(issue), first page–last page. https://doi.org/xxxxx
Scientific writing is clear, concise and precise. Use one idea per paragraph, start each paragraph with a topic sentence, define terms before using them, and use the same name for a variable throughout. You may use “we” for decisions your group made together.
Numbers: write numbers below 10 in words (“three questionnaires”, “five groups”) and numbers 10 and above in digits (“12 items”, “48 participants”). There are some important exceptions. Always use digits for:

statistics, decimals, percentages and ratios (M = 3.42, 25%)
numbers with a unit of measurement or time (“2 hours of screen time”, “5 min”)
ages, scores and points on a scale (“aged 19”, “a 5-point scale”, “rated from 1 to 7”)

Never start a sentence with a digit. Either write the number in words (“Forty-eight participants took part.”) or rephrase the sentence (“The sample included 48 participants.”).
Tense at a glance








Section
Past tense for…
Present tense for…




Abstract
what you did and found
your conclusion


Introduction
specific earlier studies; your hypotheses
definitions, theories, established knowledge


Method
everything you and participants did
describing a questionnaire that still exists


Results
your findings
pointing to tables and figures


Discussion
your findings and those of other studies
interpretation, implications, take-home message



For further guidance see the APA Style Guide - Tense






NoteWhy APA does it this way




Heading levels: consistent heading levels show the structure of the report at a glance, so readers can find any section in any APA paper.
Alphabetical order and hanging indent: the author’s surname stands out, so readers can quickly find the full reference for any in-text citation.
“et al.” for three or more authors: this keeps in-text citations short, while the reference list gives every author’s name in full.

For further guidance see the APA Style Guide - References




Final checklist
Use this to check your report against the six marking criteria before you submit.
1 · Introduction

The concepts are defined in a way that matches the measures.
There is a theory or mechanism for why the variables might be related.
The research question follows from the literature.
Both H0 and H1 are stated, and any predicted direction is justified.

2 · Method

Participants, Measures and Procedure subheadings are included.
Sample size, recruitment and demographics are reported.
Each measure is described and scored clearly, and you’ve explained why it suits the variable.
The procedure says how long it took and how ethical issues were handled.

3 · Results

Descriptive statistics are reported, and tables and figures are formatted in APA style.
The checks you were taught are reported.
The correlation is reported in APA format, with a 95% CI.
You say whether you reject or fail to reject H0 (never “accept”), and what this means for H1.
All the code runs, and the numbers in the text match the output.

4 · Discussion

The finding is related to the literature.
Limitations are specific and explain their consequences.
There is no causal language.
There is a clear take-home message.

5 · Alignment

The hypotheses and the take-home message match.
Everything in the method was set up in the introduction.
The discussion conclusions are supported by the results.

6 · Scientific writing and APA

The report uses the PSYC4141 Quarto template, with its headings kept.
Your student ID, not your name, is in the author field.
The report is within 1500 words.
The tense is consistent and correct in each section (no future tense left over from the pre-registration).
Numbers below 10 are in words and 10 and above in digits, except for statistics, measurements, ages and scale points.
Statistics are formatted in APA style.
Citations and references follow APA 7.
The writing is clear and concise.

You can download this checklist here.

title: Introduction to Psychological Research
text:
Welcome
Welcome to the PSYC4141 material for the academic year 2026-2027!
How do we determine what is a true finding in psychological science? How do we know which theories are well supported by evidence? This module introduces you to rigorous and transparent scientific practices. You will develop systematic ways of thinking about and approaching real-world issues. Using modern techniques, you will learn how to collect, present and analyse data. We will introduce key concepts and practices of research design and data analysis through lectures. Practical laboratory classes will teach you how to design studies, handle data, perform statistical analyses and report your findings. The laboratory classes will be hands-on, giving you direct experience of all stages of a research project, including the use of specialised software. Topics covered will include questionnaire design, collecting and working with observational data, and looking at relationships between variables using correlation and regression analysis.


Working at your own pace and seeking help
We have carefully prepared and refined the lab materials in this course over several years, and we feel that the pace of the materials is just about right for our students. Some students will complete them more quickly, and others more slowly - both of these scenarios are absolutely fine. You should work at the pace that suits you best, making sure you understand the materials before you move forward.
It is fairly inevitable that you will get stuck on the lab materials in this module at some point. This might be in Week 1, Week 2, or later. When you do, it’s important you reach out for help:

Ask your friends on your table. We’ve designed this teaching space to help collaborative work. You are encouraged to work with other students. Make sure you ask others to explain how they’ve solved an exercise. Make sure you help out others where you can. Always make sure you understand the code and the exercise; don’t simply be satisfied that you’ve got the right answer.
Ask a GTA or Lecturer. Our Graduate Teaching Assistants are there to help you. There are no “stupid questions” in statistics, so just ask the GTAs any question about what you’re doing. Likewise, ask the Lecturer.
Ask on the Q&A Forum on Moodle. On the PSYC4141 moodle page you will find a Q&A Forum. This is a great way to ask a question outside of the lab sessions. It might seem scary to ask a question in the forum, but please don’t be afraid to do this. If you have a question, you can bet 30+ other students also have the same question! So by asking the question on the forum, you help out many more people on the module. A friendly GTA or Lecturer will be along to answer the question as soon as possible (we aim for within 48 hours during the working week).
Ask during live online Q & A session. Each week we hold an online “Q&A” session where we will try and resolve any general queries and problems. It’s an ideal time to discuss things that students are struggling with or confused about, and can share ideas and answers. You can ask on the discussion forum above and then we might be able to pick up the issues and discuss them, but also you can ask in the session itself.

Asking good questions - It’s really important that you give us as much information as you can when you ask your questions (in class and especially on the forum). It’s so much harder to help respond to “I can’t do Exercise 5 in Week 7” (because we don’t know why it is that you can’t do it) than for example “In Exercise 5 of Week 7, I’ve managed to read in the data, but the graph looks quite odd. Here is the code I’m using…”

1. The mini research project






NoteWhy do we do a mini research project?



Lectures and textbooks can only take you so far. Doing research shows you things that are hard to appreciate any other way.
You see how ideas become measurable. From the inside, you see how researchers turn abstract ideas into measurable variables: how instructions are worded, questions are designed and responses are recorded. You may also notice how your own expectations shape what you do. These are the issues you’ll need to think critically about in your own designs, such as demand characteristics, operationalisation and measurement validity.
You see ethics in practice. Information sheets, informed consent, the right to withdraw and debriefing make more sense once you’ve implemented them.
You see why sample size and representativeness matter. Your own research will depend on others choosing to take part, and the project gives you a first-hand sense of that.
In short, the mini project helps you become a better researcher by connecting what you learn in class to real research practice.

4. Measuring mind wandering and screen time






Important



With your group you need to decide how to measure the variables you’ve specified in your research question. In this module we focus on using questionnaires to measure constructs.
The questionnaire needs to be:

open access (that is, openly available and free to use);
accompanied by a peer-reviewed article that discusses the construction, validity and reliability of the questionnaire.

Below I’ve listed some examples, but you can propose a different questionnaire you have found in the literature as long as it satisfies the above criteria. Asking people to report (a specific aspect of) their screen-time as recorded in a screentime app is also acceptable.








Tip



Fife-Schaw, C. (2020). 14: Questionnaire design. In G. M. Breakwell, D. B. Wright, & J. Barnett (Eds.), Research methods in psychology (5th ed., pp. 119–138). SAGE Publications. Recommended

This chapter provides a useful overview of things to consider when setting up a questionnaire study.









Tip



All reading is accessible via the library. You can go to Moodle -> Library Resources -> Resource List or you can follow this link.


Examples of papers that discuss questionnaires that measure mind wandering
Carriere, J. S. A., Seli, P., & Smilek, D. (2013). Wandering in both mind and body: Individual differences in mind wandering and inattention predict fidgeting. Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology/Revue canadienne de psychologie expérimentale, 67(1), 19–31. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031438

Carriere et al. (2013) capture two forms of mind wandering using the Mind Wandering: Spontaneous (MW-S) and Mind Wandering: Deliberate (MW-D) scales.

Mrazek, M. D., Phillips, D. T., Franklin, M. S., Broadway, J. M., & Schooler, J. W. (2013). Young and restless: Validation of the Mind-Wandering Questionnaire (MWQ) reveals disruptive impact of mind-wandering for youth. Frontiers in Psychology, 4, Article 560. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00560

Mrazek et al. (2013) created a 5-item Mind-Wandering Questionnaire (MWQ) and showed across four studies that people who score higher on it report more task-unrelated thoughts during a reading test.

Schubert, A.-L., Frischkorn, G. T., Sadus, K., Welhaf, M. S., Kane, M. J., & Rummel, J. (2024). The brief mind wandering three-factor scale (BMW-3). Behavior Research Methods, 56(8), 8720–8744. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-024-02500-6

During the first weeks of term, during the lab session you worked with some publicly available data from a research project on mind wandering carried out by Schubert and colleagues (Schubert et al., 2024). They created a 12-item questionnaire that measures how often your mind wanders without meaning to, how often you let it wander on purpose, and how aware you are when it happens.

Examples of papers on measuring aspects of screen time
In addition to the paper by Kaye et al. (2020) referred to in the section with key readings (Section 2), the following papers are good examples of papers that focus on a specific aspect of screen time.
Baumgartner, S. E., Lemmens, J. S., Weeda, W. D., & Huizinga, M. (2017). Measuring media multitasking: Development of a short measure of media multitasking for adolescents. Journal of Media Psychology, 29(4), 188–197. https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-1105/a000167

Baumgartner et al. (2017) developed a short media multitasking measure (MMM-S) – measuring the simultaneous use of two or more media.

Du, J., van Koningsbruggen, G. M., & Kerkhof, P. (2018). A brief measure of social media self-control failure. Computers in Human Behavior, 84, 68–75. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2018.02.002

Du et al. (2018) developed a 3-item scale, the Social Media Self-Control Failure (SMSCF) scale, to measure how often people give in to social media temptations.

Marty-Dugas, J., Ralph, B. C., Oakman, J. M., & Smilek, D. (2018). The relation between smartphone use and everyday inattention. Psychology of Consciousness: Theory, Research, and Practice, 5(1), 46. https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/cns0000131

Marty-Dugas et al. (2018) developed two different measures of smartphone use (general and absent-minded) and explore relationships with measures of everyday inattention.

Ohme, J., Araujo, T., de Vreese, C. H., & Piotrowski, J. T. (2021). Mobile data donations: Assessing self-report accuracy and sample biases with the iOS Screen Time function. Mobile Media & Communication, 9(2), 293-313. https://doi.org/10.1177/2050157920959106

Ohme et al. (2021) present a new methodological approach: mobile data donations using screenshots of the iOS Screen Time function. They assesses its feasibility, sample biases, and the accuracy of self-reported smartphone usage compared to log data in a general population sample of Dutch citizens.

text:
5. Pre-register your research question, hypotheses and measures and using the feedback






TipWhy pre-register?



Pre-registration means writing down your research question, hypotheses and measures before you collect any data. It is increasingly common in psychology because it:

makes you commit to a clear plan, so you can tell the difference between what you predicted and what you discovered along the way
guards against changing your hypotheses or analyses after seeing the results, which can make findings look stronger than they are
makes your reasoning transparent, so others can see what you set out to do and why
gives you a chance to get feedback on your plan while you can still change it

Here, it also means that you have settled the key decisions for your study before you start building it.



What your group needs to do
Each group needs to:

Refine the research topic to focus on specific aspects of the key concepts of mind wandering and screen time.
Formulate a clear and specific research question.
Write a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis.
Specify how you are proposing to measure the key constructs.

More information on how to do this, and suggested papers about questionnaires you could use, can be found in the sections How to write a good research question … and appropriate hypotheses? and Measuring mind wandering and screen time.
Once you have made these decisions as a group, one of you needs to complete the pre-registration form. Please check the Moodle announcement for the link to the form and the deadline.


Feedback on your pre-registrations
Thank you for submitting your pre-registrations. The module coordinator has read through your pre-registrations and given each group individual feedback. Many of you made a good start. Below, a summary of the most common issues, with do’s and don’ts, that you can check your own project against. Nearly all of them come back to one idea: your research question, definitions, measures and hypotheses need to describe the same thing, that is they need to align.

Keep a golden thread: question, concept, measure, hypothesis
The most common issue was a mismatch between what the research question says you are studying and what your questionnaire or measure actually captures. Before you finalise anything, check each link in the chain:

Does the research question name the specific constructs you are measuring, in the same terms that the questionnaires use?
Does each measure capture the construct as you have defined it, not a related one?
Do the hypotheses follow directly from the research question and refer to the same variables?







Tip



If you change one part (for example, you switch your screen time measure), you will usually need to reformulate the research question and the hypotheses to match.




Measure mind wandering, not related concepts
The assignment is to investigate (an aspect of) mind wandering. Several research questions and answers to ‘What aspect of mind wandering are you proposing to investigate?’ referred to concepts that are related to mind wandering but are not the same thing, such as:

attention span, sustained attention, lack of focus, poor attentional control
distracted behaviour, phone checking
daydreaming
information retention, quality or amount of notes, work output, effort

In everyday language these may sound similar, but in the scientific literature they are separate constructs. Some of them (like notes or work output) are likely consequences of mind wandering rather than mind wandering itself. Keep this in mind when you describe findings from the literature in your report: make sure the studies you cite actually looked at mind wandering. Smallwood and Schooler (2015) explain how mind wandering is defined and measured, so re-read it if you are unsure.






TipEasy access to readings



All reading is accessible via the library. You can go to Moodle -> Library Resources -> Resource List or you can follow this link.




Be specific about which type of mind wandering
The questionnaires differ in what they measure:

Mrazek et al. (2013) measures mind wandering in general. It does not distinguish intentional/deliberate from unintentional/spontaneous mind wandering.
Carriere et al. (2013) measures spontaneous and deliberate mind wandering. These terms are used interchangeably in the literature with unintentional and intentional, but it is neater to use the terms from your questionnaire in your research question, hypotheses and report.
Schubert et al. (2024) measures intentional mind wandering, unintentional mind wandering and meta-awareness of mind wandering.

What this means for you:

If your research question says ‘mind wandering’, that is fine only if you are measuring mind wandering in general. If you want to focus on one type, say so in the research question and choose a questionnaire that can measure it.
If you use all three aspects of the Schubert questionnaire, think about whether you expect the same or a different relationship between screen time and each aspect, and write your hypotheses accordingly. You may also choose to use only the questions for one or two aspects.
Use the questionnaire items exactly as written. Changing the items would invalidate the questionnaire and make it difficult to compare your results with other studies.



If you study mind wandering in a specific context, adapt the instructions carefully
Many groups added a context to the research question (during lectures, independent study, academic settings, the morning). That is a good way to make a question more specific, but the questionnaires are written to ask about everyday mind wandering, so you have to deal with that. The simplest option is to use the questionnaire developed by Carriere et al. (as the phrasing of their questions still make sense if you change the context) and make a small change to the instruction that participants see, not to the items themselves. Specifically, Carriere et al. ask participants to reflect on their ‘everyday mind wandering’; you could instead ask about mind wandering ‘while attending university lectures’. If you do this:

Define the context for participants (for example, are in-person and pre-recorded lectures included? What counts as independent study or an academic session?). Give examples.
Make sure the questions still make sense in that context.
Justify in your report why you chose the context and describe how you adapted the instruction.

The same logic applies to screen time: if you are interested in a particular time of day (such as the morning scroll), you can build that into the instruction.


Decide how you will measure screen time, and make sure it matches your question
This was the second most common issue, and we recognise this may have partly come about by the way the module coordinator phrased parts of the pre-registration form. Many groups described screen time as a specific behaviour (for example, time spent on TikTok or time watching short-form content) but selected a questionnaire that measures something different:

Baumgartner et al. (2017) measures media multitasking;
Du et al. (2018) measures social media self-control failure;
Marty-Dugas et al. (2018) measures general and absent-minded smartphone use.

These are all related to screen time, but none of them is the same as the amount of time people spend on an app or a type of content. Please decide which of the following you will do, and make your research question and hypotheses fit that decision:

Ask participants to log their time on particular apps (a direct but self-reported measure of time spent).
Use a questionnaire (which measures a particular behaviour or experience linked to screen time, not time spent).
Use both. This is allowed, but you must explain why in your introduction, and consider whether you expect the same or different associations with mind wandering for each measure.

If you ask participants to log their usage: - Ask for minutes, not hours. 125 minutes is easier to work with than ‘2 hours and 5 minutes’. - Give clear instructions on where to find the information on their phone, which apps to include and over which period (for example, yesterday or the past week). - Define the category you are asking about. What counts as social media or short-form content? Does anything you can send messages on count? - Keep it as a continuous variable. You don’t need to split people into high and low users as we are using a correlational design (not a group comparison design) - We can check whether it is possible on Gorilla to ask participants to upload a screenshot as a check, in addition to the logged minutes.


Hypotheses: correlational wording, correct logic
Our design is correlational, so the wording of your hypotheses has to reflect that.
Do:

State the null hypothesis as: there is no association (correlation) between X and Y.
State the alternative hypothesis as: there is an association between X and Y (non-directional), or there is a positive (as X goes up, Y goes up) or negative (as X goes up, Y goes down) association (directional).
Be specific if you have several measures or aspects of mind wandering: say what you expect for each.
In your report, justify whether your hypothesis is directional or non-directional using studies from the literature.

Don’t:

Use causal language such as ‘effect on’, ’ more of X increases Y’, ‘more of X leads to’ or ‘X causes Y’. With a correlational design, we cannot know whether X causes Y, Y causes X, or something else drives both.
Swap the null and alternative hypotheses. The null states there is no association.
Frame the question as a group comparison (for example, more or less than 4 hours). We are using correlation, so keep screen time continuous.
Add things that don’t come out of your measures (such as a score out of 10).



Keep the scope manageable
Some research questions contained several questions in one (for example, social media use and attention, social media use and information retention, and an age comparison). Choose one relationship and one population. When you choose a population, check your hidden assumptions (for example, do people in this group use the platform you are asking about?) and think about how you will recruit them.






TipQuick checklist



Use the checklist below to check your project:

My research question names the specific constructs I am measuring, not broader or related ones.
My definition of mind wandering and my questionnaire match.
My screen time measure matches how I describe screen time in the research question.
If I adapted instructions for a context, I have defined the context and can justify the choice.
My hypotheses use correlational language, have the null and alternative the right way round, and fit my measures.
My question is small enough to answer with one correlational design.









ImportantHow to use the feedback



You can use this feedback in two ways:

To build your study on Gorilla. The feedback helps you check that the measures you build are the ones you decided on, and what you need to know before you start. Please refer to the section on Building your study on Gorilla for step by step guidance.
To write the introduction for your research report. The same decisions shape the introduction of your research report, which needs to make an argument for why your study makes sense and why it is designed the way it is. Please refer to the section on Building the rationale for your study to help you plan this.

7. Building your study on Gorilla

Getting set up:
To build your group’s questionnaire study on Gorilla, each group needs to clone an example project and then amend that project. The example project contains the following components:

Participant information sheet
Consent form
Debrief sheet


What you need to do as a group:

One member of your group needs to sign in to Gorilla and carry out assignment 1: Clone the example project and add collaborators. Information on how to clone a project is here.
That same group member then needs to add the other group members as collaborators. Information on how to add collaborators is here.




Preparing your study for Gorilla
Now that you have made your key decisions, the next step is to build your study on Gorilla. Before you open Gorilla, work through the Preparing your study for Gorilla activity as a group. It takes about an hour and helps you check that what you build matches what you decided to measure, and that you have all the information you need to build it.
By the end, your group will have a build sheet for three questionnaires:

Mind wandering
Screen time
Demographics, adapted to the people you are recruiting

The activity has four steps:

Write down what you decided. Summarise your research question, population, measures and hypotheses, and check that they all describe the same thing.
Complete a build sheet for each measure. For each questionnaire, work out the information you need before building it, such as the exact items, instructions, response scales and scoring.
Plan your data. List the variables you will collect and decide the order in which participants see the questionnaires.
Build, check and test. Build the questionnaires in your cloned Gorilla project, check that you are using the correct participant information sheet, consent form and debrief sheet, and test each questionnaire to make sure it looks as expected.

The Preparing your study for Gorilla document has the full instructions, worked examples, and boxes for your group to fill in. Download it and complete it as a group before you start building.


Building your own measures
Once you all have a Gorilla account, have cloned the example project and have added all group memebers as collaborators, and have completed the Preparing your study for Gorilla activity in the Section 7.2, you are ready to start adding your own measures to measure demographics, mind wandering and screen time.






Tip



Guidance on how to do that can be found in the section above on Learning about the Gorilla platform here.
The Gorilla reference guide on how to use their Questionnaire builder is also useful.








TipChecklist 1: Before you build the individual measures



Check that everything below is in place before you start building your three questionnaires in Gorilla.
Your decisions

My research question, definitions, measures and hypotheses all describe the same thing.
I know who we are recruiting, including the age range and any other criteria for taking part.

Mind wandering questionnaire

We know which questionnaire and which aspect of mind wandering we are measuring.
We have the exact wording of every item, copied from the paper.
We have the instruction wording, including any adaptation for a context, and have defined the context.
We have the response scale and labels, exactly as published.
We know how the score is calculated, including any reverse-scored items.

Screen time measure

We have decided whether to use a usage log, a questionnaire or both.
We have defined exactly what counts as screen time, and which time period we are asking about.
We have written the exact question wording, and clear instructions for where participants find the information.

text:
Lectures
Last week, you looked at some of the bigger questions that sit behind psychological science: how theories are linked to observable evidence, why our observations provide estimates rather than direct access to the “truth”, and why the complexity and variability of human behaviour matter.
This week, we move from those ideas to some of the practical tools that allow us to gather and make sense of evidence. We’ll look at how psychological concepts can be represented as data, and how choices about measurement, summary and visualisation shape the evidence we use to evaluate scientific claims.

The lectures are grouped into section A and B (relating to the two strands of learning stated above). Each section is split into short videos so you can work through them at your own pace. It’s a good idea to take notes as you go and to have a 10-minute break between section A and section B.






NoteA note about the recordings



The recordings were originally delivered by Prof John Towse and have been selected and reorganised for this week’s teaching. If you hear references to a different week or to something covered “last week” don’t worry about these references! I’ve reviewed the materials and you will never be expected to know anything that you haven’t yet covered. All questions should be posted on the discussion forum and will be answered by Carly. Please do not contact John about his content.








TipQuestions?



Make a note of questions as you work through the material. These might be answered later in the recordings, or in your lab. Otherwise, please bring them to the live online Q&A session on Friday or post them on the Q&A forum on Moodle.



Section A: Psychological measurement and central tendency
You can watch the lecture for the video using the video playback windows shown next. Section A is broken into three parts that should be watched in sequence:

Types of data
Scales of measurement
Central tendency and notations

Download the slides for sections A and B in one go here. The transcript for all the videos is here.






TipDownloading files



If the file doesn’t download when you click on it, try right-clicking on it instead. You should than see multiple options and you can select ‘Download linked file’.


1. Types of data (~10 minutes)
What types of data can we use to measure psychological concepts that we are interested in? This includes nominal and numerical data.

2. Scales of Measurement (~9 minutes) Four different scales that we commonly use to measure our data. These include nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio.

3. Measures of central tendency and key notations (~10 minutes) Why measurement matters, and how to describe your data using numbers and appropriate measures. This includes the mean, median and mode.







TipTake a break!



Before continuing, we recommend you take a 15-minute break away from your computer. Remember to note down any questions to bring to the Q&A, lab or discussion forum whilst you’re watching the lectures.




Section B: Variability and distributions
Section B is broken into four parts that should be watched in sequence:

Variability in numbers
Variability in words
The standard deviation and distribution curves
The normal distribution curve

1. Variability in numbers (~19 minutes) Why does variability or ‘spread’ in our data matter? How can we measure and express variability using numbers? This includes range, interquartile range, deviance, variance and standard deviation.

2. Variability in words (~5 minutes) A short reflection on what numerical measures of variability can actually tell us about our data.







TipFormulae and calculations



John has just introduced the notion of using calculations to measure variability and the broader concepts behind them. You can download the key formulae for calculating variance and standard deviation and other measures here You may come across slightly different versions of these formulae (computational and conceptual) so it is useful to be aware of them. You do not need to memorise these formulae. The important thing is to understand what each measure tells us about our data and the basic idea behind how it is calculated. In the next recording, John will take you through a worked example of calculating a standard deviation.


3. The standard deviation and distribution curves (~15 minutes) An example of how to calculate standard deviation, and how we can look at variability visually using histogram plots. An overview of the shape of data distributions, with features including symmetry, skew, and bimodality.

4. The normal distribution (~9 minutes) Basic properties of the normal distribution curve and linking central tendency and standard deviation to the normal curve.

Pre-lab activities
The lecture material is designed to deliver important ideas and procedures for learning about psychological science and analysis. Pre-lab material is then designed to help consolidate this learning, or enhance, expand and apply it in ways that set the scene for the lab session activity. We want to prepare you to be ready to go in the session itself and make the most of your time there.

Pre-lab activity 1: From psychological claims to measurements
Last week, you considered psychological claims that we might encounter in everyday life. One example is the claim that “screen time negatively impacts mental health in adolescents”. Before we could investigate this claim, we would need to decide what we actually mean by screen time and how we could turn that concept into something we can observe and measure.
One simple approach might be to ask people: “Approximately how many hours did you spend looking at a screen yesterday?”
Imagine we asked a small group of adolescents and received the following sample of responses:
6 8 5 9 7 4 11 6 7 8 10 5 6 12 7 8 4 9 6 7 14 5 8 6 10 7 3 9
Take a moment to think about what these numbers actually represent.






NotePre-lab question 1




What scale of measurement best describes the number of hours of screen time reported here?



Nominal
Ordinal
Interval
Ratio







TipShow answer





d. Ratio. Time measured in hours has equal intervals, and zero hours represents the absence of the measured quantity. This means that differences and ratios between values are meaningful.





Once we have collected observations like these, how can we describe them in a useful way? One way is to summarise the data to find the mean or average value. You’ll learn how to do that in RStudio during the lab, but for now, have a look at the website app: Describing and Exploring Quantitative Variables: https://istats.shinyapps.io/EDA_quantitative/. The website should open in a new window. You may be offered a free trial of the ‘Art of Stat Mobile App’; you can dismiss that.
Choose the following options:

Under ‘Enter Data’, select ‘Your Own’
Under ‘Name of Variable’, enter a sensible label (such as ‘Screen time’)
Under ‘Enter observations’, add the numbers of the observations
Under ‘Choose Type of Plot’, click the box to select a ‘Histogram’.

Now have a look:

On the right, you’ll see key descriptive statistics such as the mean and the standard deviation (Std. Dev.).
Below it, you can see a histogram. If the histogram looks funny, try adjusting the bin size.







NoteWhat is a histogram?



A histogram is a graph that shows how the values of a continuous (or finely measured) variable are distributed. The values are divided into consecutive, equal-width intervals called bins, and a bar is drawn for each bin with its height showing how many observations fall inside it (or the proportion or density). Because the bins are adjacent, the bars touch, which distinguishes a histogram from a bar chart of separate categories. Histograms make it easy to see the shape of a distribution, including its centre, spread, skew, and any outliers or multiple peaks.


Play around:

What happens if you add more observations? How does it change the mean and the standard deviation? What happens to the histogram?
Try adding 10 observations of lower screen time values.
Try adding an impossibly large observation, like 89. That is, of course, far larger than there are hours in the day, but data entry errors like that do happen. How does it effect the mean and the standard deviation?
You can also click the option to see a boxplot as well as a histogram. Can you work out how key descriptive statistics are represented in a boxplot?







NotePre-lab question 2




The mean reported screen time in this sample was approximately 7.4 hours. Which of the following would NOT be justified from these data?



Participants reported an average of 7.4 hours of screen time.
There was variation in reported screen time between participants.
Adolescents who use screens more have poorer mental health.
Some participants reported more screen time than others.







TipShow answer





c. Here, our measure of screen time is self-reported hours of screen use on one day. We have not measured mental health, so these observations cannot tell us whether greater screen use is associated with poorer mental health. Our measure of “screen time” is also only one possible way of representing a complex behaviour. For example, it does not distinguish between different activities or content, such as studying, gaming, messaging friends or watching videos. This illustrates an important challenge in psychological science: the questions and theories we are interested in are often complex, while the data we collect are particular observations produced by the choices we make about what and how to measure. So, even when we can accurately describe a set of observations, we still need to be careful about what those observations allow us to conclude.











NotePre-lab question 3




If two sets of data have exactly the same mean, what can we conclude about their variability?



They must have the same variability
They must have the same standard deviation
One must have a larger range
We cannot tell from the mean alone







TipShow answer





d.

Lectures
Last week, we explored how two measures can vary together. You practised visualising the relationship using scatterplots and estimating Pearson’s \(r\). We also talked about how we respect participants’ choices, collect and protect appropriate data, and interpret and communicate research findings responsibly.
This week, we learn about hypothesis testing and significance testing and apply this to correlation analysis. We will also practise reporting correlation analysis following APA conventions.
We will make a start with the group project.







Important



Please watch the lecture material, complete the essential reading and then the pre-lab activities before attending your lab. As a reminder, the lectures and pre-labs introduce the concepts and give you some initial practice, and the lab gives you the opportunity to apply these skills in-person with our support.

Section A: Hypothesis testing, significance testing
You can watch the lecture for the video using the video playback windows shown next. Our lecture on hypothesis testing and significance testing, shown next, is split into six short parts that you should watch in sequence.


1. Hypothesis testing and significance testing (~70 minutes in total)
You can download the lecture slides as a .html file you can open in any browser.
The slides end with a references list but don’t worry about reading what’s in the references list, we give you recommended readings in Section 2.






Tip



The slides presented in the next videos can be downloaded as a web page: hypothesis-testing-significance.html.

Lecture slides

When you download the file, double click on it to open it in your usual web browser for viewing.
There are many slides but not all slides are discussed in-depth in the lecture, some are there to help to visually support transitions between points.


Next, you can see the lecture elements. We recommend that you watch them in the order they are shown in.
1.1. We are going to learn about hypothesis or significance testing (~5 minutes). This is a challenging topic. We can meet this challenge by enriching our perspectives to take in historical, philosophical, and psychological viewpoints.


    


1.2. What is NHST and where does it come from? (~13 minutes). We are going to learn about hypothesis testing and significance from two different perspectives: (1.) The perspective of an individual researcher, asking what they can learn from the evidence from their study. (2.) The perspective of someone looking at errors that we (in general) could make as we make decisions based on the evidence from multiple repeated studies. We begin with the first perspective, based on Ronald Fisher’s ideas.

    


1.3. Demonstration: significance testing (~20 minutes). We have outlined the logic of the significance test in words. But it is often easier to understand the logic if we see how the ideas work in practice.

    


1.4. Hypothesis testing (~10 minutes). We switch to a different philosophy and a different view of the psychology of researchers. We take a second perspective, grounded in thinking about error rates, based on the ideas of Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson.

    


1.5. Seeing the Neyman-Pearson approach at work (24 minutes). To help us to build understanding, we work through demonstrations that build on realistic simulations of the kind of evidence we collect in psychological studies of correlation.

    


1.6. Summary (8 minutes). Two ways of thinking clearly about evidence. The impacts on how we write about and think about research as psychologists.

Lab activity 2: Hypothesis testing for correlations – getting ready

Background
This week, we are going to work with data that we have generated (through simulations) but which are based on data from a real project looking at how psychologists measure vocabulary knowledge.
Hanke Vermeiren and colleagues (Vermeiren et al., 2023) completed a series of studies to develop a vocabulary test for English-speaking university students. Among the tests they developed were measures of vocabulary knowledge (what you know about word meanings) and of reading experience (print exposure, based on recognition of author names). They share information on the tests through the repository: https://osf.io/ef3s4/overview.






Tip



I talk about this study in the lecture on Hypothesis testing, significance testing because there are good reasons to think we might see correlations between measures of vocabulary knowledge and measures of reading experience.


Reference
Vermeiren, H., Vandendaele, A., & Brysbaert, M. (2023). Validated tests for language research with university students whose native language is English: Tests of vocabulary, general knowledge, author recognition, and reading comprehension. Behavior Research Methods, 55(3), 1036–1068. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-022-01856-x.


Aims of the activity

Download and organise your files
Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio
Read in the data

These files all hold scores on tests of vocabulary knowledge or of reading experience.

Different (simulated) participants’ scores are on different rows of each spreadsheet.
Different kinds of scores are in different columns of each spreadsheet.

Column names are shown at the top of the columns. The names encode information about what the column data are about in a [..].[..].[..].[..] four-part naming scheme:

[what test? vocabulary or experience].[is r positive or negative or zero?].[is r large, medium, small in size?].[how big is the participant sample? small (30) medium (100) large (1000)]

You will often need to change things like:
The colour of points








Figure 1: Scatterplots showing the relationship between reading experience and vocabulary. Points vary in colour











NoteClick here to see how to change the colour of points





The important change is to add colour: geom_point(colour = ...)

ggplot(data = thirty, aes(x = exper.pos.sma.sma, y = vocab.pos.sma.sma)) +
  geom_point(colour = "limegreen") +
