We created a Shiny web app so that you can reflect critically on some of the ideas we discussed in the lecture, and that you can see play out in the exercises you have just done.






TipAccess the app here



Access the app by clicking on this link
The app works in Chrome but not (yet) in Safari. It is under development.
You can copy the link https://robayedavies.github.io/teaching-nhst-corr-demo-shiny/ and paste it into Chrome to access the app there, if you are not already using Chrome.
Paste the link into Chrome, or click to access (if you are already working in Chrome), wait a few seconds, and you should see a webpage somewhat like the image shown next.





A shiny web app for exploring correlations


The app allows you to control:

The number of people tested: Participants per study (N) button.
The correlation: Population correlation (r) slider.
You can get new samples as many time as you like: Draw new samples button.







Tip



What we are doing when we do significance testing is explained in the lectures. Watch the videos and come back if you have not done this already.

The Our observed dataset on the left shows a single simulated dataset with the correlation and the participant sample you selected.
The Six more datasets in the middle show six further datasets with the same correlation, but each shows how the correlation can vary, given different random samples of data.


These datasets are simulated every time you click on the Participants per study (N) button or move the Population correlation (r) slider button to a new correlation value.
You can also get new simulations each time you click on the Draw new samples button (see top right of the webpage.)


The piles-of-dots on the top right of the web page show comparisons between the \(r\) correlation for Our observed dataset and distributions of \(r\) correlations for (2.) lots of samples, taken at random, assuming the null hypothesis H0 is true.
The piles-of-dots on the bottom right of the web page show comparisons between the \(r\) correlation for the “observed” dataset and distributions of \(r\) correlations for (2.) lots of samples, taken at random, assuming the alternative hypothesis HA is true.

Have a play with the web app and then answer the following questions.



Pick any correlation value using the Population correlation (r) slider. Compare the scatterplot for 1. Our observed dataset with the six scatterplots for 2. Six more datasets, same population. Look at the plots and compare:


the scatter (spread) of points
the trend shown by the points (are high experience values associated with high vocabulary scores, or not).

Here’s the question for reflection: What does this comparison tell you about the ways in which things like association vary between different samples of people?

Discuss your answer with your group, and write a brief reflection down in words in your .qmd.









Keeping the correlation value you selected, click on the Draw new samples button a few times.

(i.) Look at the plots every time you do this and compare:

the scatter (spread) of points
the trend shown by the points.

(ii.) Also, look at the pile-of-dots plots on the right of the screen. Notice the red line move about every time you click on the Draw new samples button.

The red line indicates the r correlation estimated for the 1. Our observed dataset sample.

Here’s the question for reflection: What does this comparison tell you about the ways in which things like association vary between different samples of people?

Discuss your answer with your group, and write a brief reflection down in words in your .qmd.









Now select a correlation of 0 by moving the Population correlation (r) slider, and click on the Draw new samples button a few times. Keep looking at the scatterplots and at r correlation and t (t-test statistic) values shown above the plots.


Note that if \(t > 2\) (roughly) we may expect the test statistic to be significant.

Here’s the question for reflection: We know for a fact that there is no true correlation in the population because we set the correlation value ourselves. What do the simulations suggest about what we may observe nevertheless in the samples we collect when we test people?

Discuss your answer with your group, and write a brief reflection down in words in your .qmd.










Now it’s time to see what happens when we vary the size of our sample. Keep the population correlation value the same: pick any correlation you like. For this exercise, a value of \(r = .30\) is illustrative. Now click on the Participants per study (N) button to reveal a drop down menu. Choose a sample size. Try this a few times: increase the sample size up to 1000. Look at three things:


Look at the scatter of points in each scatterplot;
Look at the \(r, t, p\) statistics above each plot;
Look at the pile-of-dots plots, both the piles themselves (the shape or spread of the pile) and the red line marking the observed r.

There is a lot going on but we can pick out the key insights.
Here are the questions for reflection:

You selected the correlation value yourself, so you know what the correlation should be in the different samples: what do you see?
I expect you will see the correlation values will vary across samples (as we have seen already): what happens to this variation when you go from smaller to larger samples?
How does the per-sample correlation compare to the population correlation you selected?
What do you see happen to the piles-of-dots?

Discuss your answers with your group, and write a brief reflection down in words in your .qmd.

Lab activity 3: Reminders through association
For this lab, we’re going to use data from Rogers, T. & Milkman, K. L. (2016). Reminders through association. Psychological Science, 27, 973-986. You can read the full paper online but the short version is that the authors looked at how people remember to follow through with the intention of doing something.
Although there are lots of potential reasons (e.g., some people may lack the self-control resources), Rogers and Milkman (2016) propose that some people fail to follow through simply because they forget about their good intentions. If this is the case, the authors argue, then having visual reminders to follow through on their intentions may help people remember to keep them. For example, a person may choose to put a sticker for their gym on their car window, so that every time they get in the car they remember to go to the gym.
In Study 1 by Rogers and colleagues, participants took part in an unrelated experiment but at the start of the task they were asked to return a small stack of paper clips to the reception of the building at the end of the study and if they did so the researchers would donate $1 to a charity. They were then asked if they intended to do this. Those in the reminder-through-association (RTA) condition read “Thank you! To remind you to pick up a paper clip, an elephant statuette will be sitting on the counter as you collect your payment.” This message was followed by a picture of the elephant statuette. Those in the control condition simply read “Thank you!”.
What we want to do is to run a chi-square analysis to determine whether those in the reminder-through-association condition were more likely to remember to return the paper-clips than those in the control condition.

Extract descriptive statistics

Run the chi-square analysis
Check the assumptions
Calculate the effect size
Check the adjusted standardised residuals
Write up the results

Step 3: Some data wrangling - Use filter() to keep relevant data
We need to do a little bit of wrangling to get our data into the format we need: First, we need to remove all the participants who said that they did not intend to return the paper-clips (intend = 0) as we are only interested in whether people follow through on an intention.

Action: Insert a new code chunk and use filter() to remove all participants who said that they did not intend to return the paper-clips. Can a look below for a reminder on how filter() works. Give it a go. If you’re stuck, have a look at the Code below.







TipHow does filter() work?



The filter() function allows you to select specific rows from a data frame based on one or more conditions.
For example, imagine we have a dataset containing information about participants in a psychology study, including their age and gender. We might want to select only participants who are over 18 years old.
We can do this using:
filter(data, age > 18)
Here: - data is the name of our data frame. - age > 18 is the condition we want to apply. - note these two bits of information are separated within the function by a comma. - only rows where the condition is TRUE are kept.
We can also apply multiple conditions. For example, to select participants who are over 18 and identify as a woman:
filter(data, age > 18, gender == "Woman")
When we provide multiple conditions separated by commas, filter() keeps only rows that satisfy all of the conditions.
Some useful operators for filtering data include:

age > 18

We can also use & (AND) and | (OR) to combine conditions.
For example:
filter(data, age >= 18 & age <= 30)
This selects participants aged between 18 and 30 (inclusive).

The ggplot2() package allows you to customise all aspects of your plots, so let’s tidy ours up a little bit. We’re going to do the following:

Step 7: Run the chi-square analysis
Now let’s run that chi-square analysis to see whether our impression from the plot holds up and there is a significant association between the grouping variables.

Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

results <- chisq.test(x = intent_data$condition,
y = intent_data$actualdonate,
correct = FALSE)
results






NoteHow does chisq.test() work?



results <- chisq.test(x = intent_recode$condition,        # the first grouping variable
                      y = intent_recode$actualdonate,     # the second grouping variable
                      correct = FALSE)                    # whether we want to apply the continuity correction (use if any of the expected cell frequencies < 10 in 2 x 2 table)
results


Question Step 7: What do you conclude from the output?


Step 8: Check the assumptions
The assumptions for chi-square are as follows:

The data in the cells should be frequencies, or counts of cases rather than percentages.
The levels (or categories) of the variables are mutually exclusive. That is, a particular participant fits into one and only one group of each of the variables.
Each participant may contribute data to one and only one cell. If, for example, the same participants are tested over time such that the comparisons are of the same subjects at Time 1, Time 2, Time 3, etc., then Chi-square may not be used.
The study groups must be independent. This means that a different test must be used if the two groups are related. For example, a different test must be used if the researcher’s data consists of paired samples, such as in studies in which a parent is paired with his or her child.
There are 2 variables, and both are measured as categories, usually at the nominal level. While Chi-square has no rule about limiting the number of cells (by limiting the number of categories for each variable), a very large number of cells (over 20) can make it difficult to meet assumption #6 below, and to interpret the meaning of the results.
The expected cell frequencies should be greater than 5.

Assumptions 1) to 5) should be evaluated by reviewing the design of the study. The only assumption that we need to check with R is whether all expected frequencies are greater than 5. This information is in the object in which you stored the results of the Chi-square test, under expected.

Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

results$expected
Question Step 8: What do you conclude from the output?


Step 9: Calculate the effect size
The last step before writing up the results is to calculate an effect size so that we have a standardised measure of how large the association between our grouping variables is. The effect size measure for chi-square is Cramer’s V. To calculate Cramer’s V we’re going to use the function cramers_v() from the easystats package. The code mirrors the code used for the Chi-square test itself.

Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

effect_size <- cramers_v(x = intent_data$condition,     
                         y = intent_data$actualdonate) 
effect_size
We can square the effect size (or multiple it by itself) to see how much variance in one variable is accounted for by the other variable. Use the code snippet below to square the effect size.
percentageAccountedFor <- effect_size$Cramers_v_adjusted * effect_size$Cramers_v_adjusted *100
percentageAccountedFor
Question Step 9: How large is the effect and how much variance is accounted for?


Step 10: Adjusted standardised residuals
To help interpret the relationship, it is useful to look at the adjusted standardised residuals. These are z-scores showing how many standard deviations each observed count is above or below the count expected if the variables were unrelated, so they indicate which cells differ most from expectation. Because they approximately follow a standard normal distribution, values beyond ±1.96 indicate a difference at p < .05 (two-tailed), beyond ±2.58 at p < .01, and beyond ±3.29 at p < .001.

Action: Copy the code snippet below to a new code chunk.

results$stdres   # check the adjusted standardised residuals
Question Step 10: What do you conclude from the output?

Answers





Lab activity 2

Question 1: How does Pearson’s Chi-square differ from Pearson’s correlation?






NoteQuestion 1: Answer





Pearson’s Chi-square assesses whether there is a relationship between categorical (or nominal) variables. Pearson’s correlation assesses whether there is a relationship between continuous (or interval/ratio) variables.





Question 2: Chi-square test of independence would be appropriate when testing the following questions:

What is the relationship between gender and soft drink preference?







NoteQuestion 2a: Answer





True




How do males and females compare in terms of wanting to be a psychologist when they leave school?







NoteQuestion 2b: Answer





True





Question 3: Write the chi-square formula below.






NoteQuestion 3: Answer











Question 4: What were your answers to the pre-lab activity 1 questions? Please compare them with other students at your table. Complete the Pearson’s chi-square test by hand using the data above and fill in the blanks:






NoteQuestion 4: Answer







First determine expected frequencies: Smoke/drink: (70 x 65) / 110 = 41.36 Smoke/don’t drink (70 x 45) / 110 = 28.63 Don’t smoke/drink (40 x 65) / 110 = 23.63 Don’t smoke/don’t drink (40 x 45) / 110 = 16.36
Then calculate chi-square:** Smoke/drink: (50-41.36)2 / 41.36 = 1.80 Smoke/don’t drink: (20-28.63)2 / 28.63 = 2.60 Don’t smoke/drink: (15-23.63)2 / 23.63 = 3.15 Don’t smoke/don’t drink: (25-16.36)2 / 16.36 = 4.56 1.80+2.60+3.15+4.56 = 12.11

\(\chi 2\) (1, N = 110) = 12.11, p < .001
Can you reject the null hypothesis? Yes





Question 5: Why is it recommended to opt for multiple 2 x 2 chi-squares instead of chi-squares larger than 2 x 2?






NoteQuestion 5: Answer





It is easier to interpret and such a design requires a smaller sample size.





Question 6: How could you ‘modify’ the contingency table below for chi-square analysis to aid subsequent interpretation of the data/results?






NoteQuestion 6: Answer






By combining ‘interested’ and ‘somewhat interested’ or by partitioning (doing multiple 2 x 2 chi-squares, while using Bonferroni correction to account for running multiple tests.

Question Step 3

How many participants were removed because they didn’t intend to return the paper-clips?







NoteQuestion Step 3: Answer





10 participants. The table ‘intent_data’ contains 87 observations, after we have applied the filter() function to include only those participants who did intend to return the paper-clips, the table contains 77 observations.





Questions Step 5

NoteQuestions Step 5: Answers

16
10

Questions Step 6

What does position = "dodge" do? Remove it and rerun the code to find out.
Describe the pattern in the data in your own words.







NoteQuestions Step 6: Answers






“dodge” places the bars next to each other, rather than on top of each other.
The number of participants in the reminders-through-association condition who donated seems to be substantially higher than participants in that condition who did not donate. Numbers of participants in the control condition who did and did not donate is more similar.






Question Step 7
What do you conclude from the output?






NoteQuestion Step 7: Answer





As p is smaller than .005, you can conclude that there is a significant association between the grouping variables.





Question Step 8
What do you conclude from the output?






NoteQuestion Step 8: Answer





The expected frequencies in all cells are greater than 5. The data therefore meet the assumption.





Questions Step 9
How large is the effect and how much variance is accounted for?






NoteQuestions Step 9: Answers





The effect size (Cramer’s V) = 0.33 and the percentage variance accounted for = 11%.





Question Step 10
What do you conclude from the output?






NoteQuestion Step 10: Answer





The adjusted standardised residuals show a significant association between condition and donating. Values beyond about ±1.96 indicate a cell that deviates from independence at roughly the .05 level (two-tailed), and ±2.87 is well past that.
The direction is clear:
RTA condition: more people donated than expected under independence (+2.87), and fewer didn’t donate than expected (-2.87).
Control condition: fewer people donated than expected (-2.87), and more didn’t donate than expected (+2.87).
The residuals are identical in magnitude and mirror each other because this is a 2x2 table. With only one degree of freedom, all four cells carry the same information, so you only need to interpret one of them. Don’t treat them as four separate findings. The adjusted standardised residuals would be more informative when interpreting a larger (e.g., 3x2) contingency table.
The residuals tell you where and in which direction the association lies.





Question Step 11
Write up the results following APA guidelines.






NoteQuestion Step 11: Answer





Those in the reminder-through-association condition performed the intended behaviour at a significantly higher rate (74%, 29 out of 39) than did those in the control condition (42%, 16 out of 38)), χ2(1, N = 77) = 8.24, p = 0.004, V = 0.33. The analysis showed that 11% of variance in intended behaviour could be accounted for by condition (reminder-through-association vs. control).

Lectures






Note



Please note that Rob may mention a different module code or different week during the lectures. I’ve reviewed the material and the content is entirely relevant to the current module.








Tip



In week 8, we aim to further develop skills in analysing and in visualising psychological data. We will do so in the context of the Clearly Understood project.
We will aim to answer the research question: What person attributes in adult readers predict success in understanding written health information?
Research questions like this can be examined using linear models.
When we do these analyses, we will need to adapt how we report the results:

we need to report information about the model we specify, identifying all predictors;
we will need to decide if the effects of one or more predictors are significant;
we will report the model fit statistics (F, R-squared) as well as coefficient estimates;
and we need to learn to write texts describing the impact of predictors.

Usually, in describing the impacts of predictors, we are required to communicate:

the direction of the effect – do values of the outcome variable increase or decrease given increasing values of the predictor?
the size of the effect – how much do values of the outcome variable increase or decrease given increasing values of the predictor?

This task of description is enabled by producing plots of the predictions we can make:

plots to show we expect the outcome to change, given different values of a predictor.









Tip



Before you go on to the activities in Section 4, watch the lectures:


The lecture for part A for this week is presented in four short parts. You can view video recordings of the lectures using Panopto, by clicking on the links shown following.

Overview (18 minutes): What we are doing in Week 8 – Exploring the power of linear models, extending their application to use multiple variables to predict people.



Using linear models to predict people (13 minutes): Coding, thinking about, and reporting linear models with multiple predictors.



Critical evaluation (15 minutes): Critically evaluating the results of analyses involving linear models.



Everything is some kind of linear model (13 minutes): Understanding just how general and powerful this method for understanding people can be.

The slides


The lectures have three main areas of focus
1. Working with the linear model with multiple predictors
We focus in-depth on how you code linear models, how you identify critical information in the results summaries, and how you report the results: the language and the style you can use in your reports.






Tip




A small change to lm() coding releases tremendous power and flexibility in how you use the analysis method.



2. Analyses are done in context so when we conduct analyses we must use contextual information
The power and flexibility of the linear model presents challenges. We must decide which predictor variables we specify in our model. This specification requires us to think about our theoretical assumptions and what they require us to include to make sense of the behaviours or the individual differences we observe when we do things like investigating what makes health information easy or difficult to understand.
3. Developing critical thinking
As we develop conceptual understanding and practical skills, we must learn to reflect critically on our analyses, and learn to critically evaluate the analyses we read about when we read research reports in the scientific literature.






Tip



Critical analysis can develop by considering

validity
measurement
generalizability



We are always working in the broader context of uncertainty:

uncertainty about the predictions we may make concerning outcomes of interest;
uncertainty given the possibility that predicted effects may vary between individuals or groups;
uncertainty given the influence of sources of randomness in how specific responses are produced.

What person attributes predict success in understanding health information?



In Week 7, we used linear models with one predictor at a time. This week (Week 8), we extend the linear model in two ways:

Step 1: Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio

Action: In a new code chunk, add the code to empty the R environment. Then add the code to load the relevant libraries. We need the following ones: here, tidyverse, easystats and ggeffects.







NoteHint






rm(list=ls()) removes all the objects (datasets, models) currently stored in the Environment (top right quadrant), so that nothing left over from earlier work, for example from Week 7, gets mixed up with this week’s work.
Use the library() function to load each package.
ggeffects is new this week. We use it in Step 7 to plot the predictions of a linear model.










TipCode





rm(list=ls())

library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(easystats)
library(ggeffects)





Step 2: Read in and inspect the data
The data file for this lab activity is study-two-general-participants.csv, the same file we used in Week 7.
You can see the columns:

participant_ID participant code;
mean.acc average accuracy of response to questions testing understanding of health guidance (varies between 0-1);
mean.self average self-rated accuracy of understanding of health guidance (varies between 1-9);
study variable coding for what study the data were collected in
AGE age in years;
HLVA health literacy test score (varies between 1-16);
SHIPLEY vocabulary knowledge test score (varies between 0-40);
FACTOR3 reading strategy survey score (varies between 0-80);
GENDER gender code;
EDUCATION education level code;
ETHNICITY ethnicity (Office National Statistics categories) code.


Action 1. In a new code chunk use read_csv() and here() to read in the data file. Give the data object a distinct name, e.g. study.two.gen. Check that you can see the object in the Environment (top right quadrant).


Action 2. Use head() and summary() to get an overview of the data.







NoteHint






The code is the same as in Week 7, but the data file is now in the 4141_wk8_lab folder.
In the summary() output, pay attention to the variables of class character. These are categorical (nominal) variables. We will use one of them as a predictor in Step 9.










TipCode





study.two.gen <- read_csv(here("4141_wk8_lab", "study-two-general-participants.csv"))

head(study.two.gen)
summary(study.two.gen)



Questions Step 2

Which variables are of class character?



Step 3: Recap – draw a histogram and a scatterplot
In Week 7, we did not look at the reading strategy variable FACTOR3. We include it in our model in Step 5, so first take a look at it, using what you learned in Week 7. If you are short of time, skip this step.

Action 1. Draw a histogram of FACTOR3. Set a binwidth, use theme_bw(), edit the labels with labs(), set the x-axis limits to the possible range of scores (0-80) with xlim(), and add a vertical line showing the mean.







TipCode





ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = FACTOR3)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Reading strategy (FACTOR3)", y = "Frequency count") +
  xlim(0, 80) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(study.two.gen$FACTOR3), colour = "red", linewidth = 1.5)
R will show the warning Removed 2 rows containing missing values (geom_bar()). This is not a problem with the data: xlim() removes the two empty bars at the very edges of the x-axis, which fall just outside the limits.




Action 2. Draw a scatterplot of the association between FACTOR3 (x-axis) and mean.acc (y-axis), and edit its appearance as you did in Week 7.







TipCode





ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = FACTOR3, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2, colour = "blue", shape = 'square') +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Reading strategy (FACTOR3)", y = "Mean accuracy") +
  xlim(0, 80) + ylim(0, 1)



Questions Step 3

What is the direction of the association between FACTOR3 and mean.acc? Does it look strong or weak?



Step 4: Revise – fit a linear model with one predictor
We start by revising how to use lm() with one predictor: the model of mean.acc and HLVA that you fitted in Week 7.

Action: In a new code chunk, use lm() to fit a model with mean.acc as the outcome and HLVA as the predictor. Then get the model summary.







TipCode





model.1 <- lm(mean.acc ~ HLVA, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.1)



In Week 7, we looked at the coefficient estimates. This week, we also look at the information at the bottom of the model summary:

Adjusted R-squared tells us how much of the variation in the outcome the model accounts for, as a proportion between 0 and 1.
F-statistic tests whether the model as a whole predicts the outcome better than a model with no predictors. It is reported with two degrees of freedom (DF) and a p-value.

Questions Step 4

What is the estimate for the coefficient of HLVA, and what does it mean in words?
Report the F-statistic (F, the two DF values and the p-value) and the Adjusted R-squared.
Explain in words what this R-squared value indicates.



Step 5: Fit a linear model with multiple predictors
Now we fit a model that includes all of these predictors at the same time: health literacy (HLVA), vocabulary knowledge (SHIPLEY), reading strategy (FACTOR3) and age in years (AGE). This is the same model as the one presented in the lectures.

Action: In a new code chunk, use lm() to fit a model with mean.acc as the outcome and HLVA, SHIPLEY, FACTOR3 and AGE as the predictors. Give the model a new name. Then get the model summary. Try to write the code yourself before you look at the Code below.







NoteHow do we add more predictors?



We list the predictor variables on the right of the tilde ~, separated by a plus sign +:
model <- lm(outcome ~ predictor.1 + predictor.2 + predictor.3, data = data.set)
summary(model)

The model summary now has one row in the Coefficients table for each predictor.
Each coefficient estimate shows the predicted change in the outcome for a one-unit increase in that predictor, while holding the other predictors constant.









TipCode





model.2 <- lm(mean.acc ~ HLVA + SHIPLEY + FACTOR3 + AGE, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.2)



Questions Step 5

Which predictors have a significant effect on mean.acc? Does this match the predictions you wrote down in Pre-lab activity 2?
Compare the HLVA estimate with the estimate in Step 4. Why do you think it has changed?
Compare the Adjusted R-squared with the model in Step 4. What does the difference tell you?
Does the AGE estimate suggest that older or younger participants were more accurate? Is the effect significant?







NoteHint






For question b: health literacy and vocabulary knowledge are both measures of language experience. How might they be related to each other? You can check the correlation between them using correlation(), as you did in Week 7.
For question d: think about what a negative estimate means for the direction of the prediction line.






Step 6: Report the results of a linear model with multiple predictors
When we report a linear model with multiple predictors, we report the model we specified (the outcome and all the predictors), the model fit statistics (F with its degrees of freedom and p-value, and Adjusted R-squared) and, for each predictor, the estimate, t, p and the direction of the effect.

Action: In your Quarto document, write a short report of the model you fitted in Step 5. Write it as plain text, not in a code chunk. Use the example in the lectures and the template in the Hint.







NoteHint





Fill in the gaps ... using the model summary from Step 5.

We fitted a linear model with mean comprehension accuracy as the outcome and health literacy (HLVA), vocabulary knowledge (SHIPLEY), reading strategy (FACTOR3) and age (years) as predictors. The model is significant overall, F(…, …) = …, p …, and explains …% of variance (adjusted R² = …). The model estimates showed that the accuracy of comprehension increased with higher levels of … (b = …, t = …, p …), …


Report the estimate as b. In the lecture slides the estimate is written as β. In APA style, β is normally used for standardised estimates, and the estimates from lm() are unstandardised, so we use b. See here for guidance on APA reporting
Round t and R-squared to two decimal places. Our estimates are small because mean.acc runs from 0 to 1, so give b to three decimal places (e.g. b = 0.003, not 0.00).
Write a leading zero for b (e.g. 0.017), but not for p or R-squared (e.g. p = .005, R² = .36), because these cannot be larger than 1.
When R shows a very small p-value (e.g. 2.87e-12), report it as p < .001.






Step 7: Plot model predictions
In Week 7, we used geom_abline() to draw a prediction line from the intercept and slope of a model with one predictor. With multiple predictors, the prediction depends on the values of all the predictors, so we use ggpredict() from the {ggeffects} library. It works out the predicted outcome across the range of one predictor, while holding the other predictors constant at their average (mean) values.

Action 1. Use ggpredict() to get the predictions for HLVA from the model you fitted in Step 5. Print the predictions by typing the name you gave them, then plot them with plot(). Do the same for SHIPLEY.







TipCode





dat.HLVA <- ggpredict(model.2, "HLVA")
dat.HLVA
plot(dat.HLVA)

dat.SHIPLEY <- ggpredict(model.2, "SHIPLEY")
dat.SHIPLEY
plot(dat.SHIPLEY)

ggpredict(model.2, "HLVA") tells R which model to use (model.2) and which predictor we want predictions for ("HLVA", in quotation marks).
The printed predictions show, under Adjusted for:, the values the other predictors are held at.
In the plot, the line shows the predicted mean.acc and the shaded band shows the 95% confidence interval.
Optional: make prediction plots for FACTOR3 and AGE in the same way.




plot() zooms the y-axis in on the range of the predictions, so each plot has a different y-axis. This can make a small effect look large.

Action 2. plot() produces a ggplot, so you can edit it like your other plots. Edit the HLVA plot using theme_bw(), labs() and ylim(), setting the y-axis to the full possible range of mean.acc (0-1).







TipCode





plot(dat.HLVA) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Health literacy (HLVA)", y = "Predicted mean accuracy", title = "") +
  ylim(0, 1)
R will show the message Scale for y is already present. Adding another scale for y, which will replace the existing scale. This is not an error: it tells you that ylim() has replaced the y-axis that plot() set.



Questions Step 7

Use the HLVA estimate from Step 5 to work out how much predicted accuracy changes between an HLVA score of 4 and a score of 14. Check your answer against the printed predictions.
The estimate for SHIPLEY is smaller than the estimate for HLVA. Does this mean that vocabulary knowledge matters less than health literacy? Compare the two prediction plots, and check their axes.



Step 8: Draw boxplots to compare groups
Next, we look at a categorical variable: education level (EDUCATION). Participants reported their education as Further (further education), Higher (higher education) or Secondary (secondary school). A boxplot shows the distribution of a numeric outcome for each group: the middle line is the median, and the box holds the middle 50% of scores.

Action: In a new code chunk, draw boxplots of mean.acc for each level of EDUCATION, with each participant’s score shown as a point.







TipCode





ggplot(data = study.two.gen, aes(x = EDUCATION, y = mean.acc)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, colour = "red", alpha = 0.1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Education level", y = "Mean accuracy") +
  ylim(0, 1)

The x variable must be categorical (EDUCATION) and the y variable numeric (mean.acc).
geom_jitter() draws a point for each participant, moved slightly left or right so that points do not sit on top of each other. height = 0 keeps each point at the participant’s real score.
outlier.shape = NA stops geom_boxplot() drawing outlying scores a second time, because they are already shown as points.
See the reference pages for geom_boxplot() and geom_jitter().




Questions Step 8

Compare the medians of the three groups, and the number of participants in each group. Why might the group sizes matter?
Optional: draw the same plot for ETHNICITY. What does it show you about the participant sample?



Step 9: Fit a linear model with a categorical predictor
lm() can include categorical variables as predictors, added to the model in exactly the same way as numeric variables.

Action 1. Fit a model with mean.acc as the outcome and HLVA, SHIPLEY, FACTOR3, AGE and EDUCATION as predictors. Give the model a new name. Then get the model summary.







TipCode





model.3 <- lm(mean.acc ~ HLVA + SHIPLEY + FACTOR3 + AGE + EDUCATION, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.3)









NoteHow does R handle a categorical predictor?




R picks one of the categories (levels) to be the reference (baseline) level. Unless you tell it otherwise, it picks the level whose name comes first in the alphabet: here, Further.
The model summary has a row for each of the other levels: EDUCATIONHigher and EDUCATIONSecondary.
Each estimate is the predicted difference in the outcome between that level and the reference level, holding the other predictors constant.

There are other ways to code categorical predictors, which you will meet in later years.



Action 2. Use ggpredict() and plot() to plot the predicted effect of EDUCATION.







TipCode





dat.EDUCATION <- ggpredict(model.3, "EDUCATION")
plot(dat.EDUCATION)



For a categorical predictor, the plot shows a dot for the predicted mean.acc of each group, and whiskers (lines) showing the 95% confidence interval: longer lines mean more uncertainty. The 95% refers to the procedure, not to one particular interval: if we repeated the study over and over, 95% of the intervals calculated in this way would contain the true value (Hoekstra et al., 2014).
Questions Step 9

Which level of EDUCATION is the reference level?
What does the estimate for EDUCATIONSecondary mean? Is it significant?
In the plot, which group has the longest whiskers? Why do you think this is?
Stretch question: in the boxplot in Step 8, the Secondary group looked noticeably less accurate than the other two groups. Why is the difference estimated in the model smaller?







Tip



You can read more about confidence intervals here:
Hoekstra, R., Morey, R. D., Rouder, J. N., & Wagenmakers, E. J. (2014). Robust misinterpretation of confidence intervals. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 21, 1157-1164.




Step 10: Extension – Can people accurately evaluate whether they understand written health information?






Important



The second research question in the Clearly Understood project is:

Can people accurately evaluate whether they correctly understand written health information?



Participants also rated how well they thought they understood each health text, on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 9 (very well), which gave us their mean.self scores. If people can evaluate their own understanding, their ratings should be associated with their tested accuracy (mean.acc).

Action 1. Fit a model with mean.self as the outcome and mean.acc as the predictor. Then fit a second model the other way round: mean.acc as the outcome and mean.self as the predictor. Give each model a different name and get the summaries.







TipCode





model.self <- lm(mean.self ~ mean.acc, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.self)

model.acc <- lm(mean.acc ~ mean.self, data = study.two.gen)
summary(model.acc)




Action 2. Use ggpredict() and plot() to plot the predictions from each model.







TipCode





dat.self <- ggpredict(model.self, "mean.acc")
plot(dat.self)

dat.acc <- ggpredict(model.acc, "mean.self")
plot(dat.acc)



Questions Step 10

In the model with mean.self as the outcome, is mean.acc a significant predictor? What does this suggest is the answer to research question 2?
Compare the two models. Why are the slope estimates so different, when the variables and the data are the same? What do you notice about the t values, p-values and R-squared values?







NoteHint






mean.acc is scaled from 0 to 1 (the proportion of questions answered correctly) and mean.self is scaled from 1 to 9 (the average rating).
A coefficient estimate is the predicted change in the outcome for a one-unit increase in the predictor. What does a one-unit increase mean for each of the two variables?

title: Foundations of Psychological Research

Welcome
Welcome to PSYC4242!
How do we decide whether two groups differ in a psychological process or behaviour? This module builds on the knowledge and skills acquired in Introduction to Psychological Research (PSYC4141). You will continue to build your understanding of rigorous and transparent scientific practices and develop your thinking of real-world issues. Using modern techniques, learn more about how to collect, present and analyse data. You will be introduced to key concepts and practices of research design and data analysis through lectures. Practical laboratory classes will teach you how to design studies, handle data, perform statistical analyses and report your findings. The laboratory classes will be hands-on, giving you direct experience with all stages of a research project, including the use of specialised software. Topics covered will include experimental design, how to decide on your study participants, comparing groups for behaviours of psychological interest and hypothesis testing.


Asking for help
We have carefully prepared and refined the lab materials in this course over several years, and we feel that the pace of the materials is just right for our students. Some students will complete them more quickly, and others more slowly - both of these scenarios are absolutely fine. You should work at the pace that suits you best, making sure you understand the materials before you move forward.
It is fairly inevitable that you will get stuck on the lab materials in this module at some point. This might be in Week 11, Week 12, or later. When you do, it’s important you reach out for help:

Ask your peers on your table. We’ve designed this teaching space to help collaborative work. You are encouraged to work with other students. Make sure you ask others to explain how they’ve solved an exercise. Make sure you help out others where you can. Always make sure you understand the code and the exercise; don’t simply be satisfied that you’ve got the right answer.
Ask a Lecturer. We are here to help you. There are no “stupid questions” in statistics, so just ask the Lecturer any question about what you’re doing.
Ask on the Q&A Forum on Moodle. On the PSYC4242 moodle page you will find a Q&A Forum. This is a great way to ask a question outside of the lab sessions. It might seem scary to ask a question in the forum, but please don’t be afraid to do this. If you have a question, you can bet 30+ other students also have the same question! So by asking the question on the forum, you help out many more people on the module. A friendly GTA or Lecturer will be along to answer the question as soon as possible (we aim for within 48 hours during the working week).
Ask during live online Q & A session. Each week we hold an online “Q&A” session where we will try and resolve any general queries and problems. It’s an ideal time to discuss things that students are struggling with or confused about. You can ask on the discussion forum above and then we might be able to pick up the issues and discuss them, but you can also ask in the session itself.
